About the author

Assoc. Prof. Benedikt Perak, PhD is Associate Professor at the Department of Cultural Studies, Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences, University of Rijeka, where he heads the Laboratory for Research on Cultural Complexity. He is co-founder of SyntAgent d.o.o. (Rijeka), a company specialising in artificial intelligence, language technologies, and data science. His research spans natural language processing, cognitive and computational linguistics, and computational approaches to cultural and communicative complexity; he has authored and co-authored numerous publications in language technologies and semantic analysis.

Foreword

This book continues reflection shaped through the courses Language, Thought, and Culture, Data Science in Cultural Studies, and Artificial Intelligence and Communication in Culture at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences in Rijeka. It aims to contribute to understanding changes in communicative practices in the age of artificial intelligence, drawing on relevant literature and a critical stance. It is intended for students of communication, linguistics, cultural studies and related fields, as well as for readers who wish to follow systematically how we communicate with systems whose linguistic capabilities grow ever more sophisticated.

Although the book as a medium no longer occupies the central place it once did, this project adopts a form that is systematically renewed — an agentically renewable book. The first edition will gradually be extended with agent-assisted information retrieval, integration of new state-of-the-art technological solutions, and critical discussion of their implications for communicative and cultural phenomena. That process remains under the author’s responsibility and control.

In that spirit, new versions of this renewable book will be published periodically on GitHub, as a concrete embodiment of its core idea: we are on the threshold of collaborative work with artificial intelligence agents.

I thank colleagues who encouraged me and made disciplined research experimentation possible, from which the insights in this book emerged. I owe special gratitude to my family and friends for their steady support and for the sense of meaningfulness they provide.

Benedikt Perak

Rijeka, 2025.

1 Introduction: Communication and the development of civilization

From the ancient, barely distinguishable voices with which the first hominids communicated, all the way to the complex linguistic tissues that permeate today’s digital spaces, communication appears as a fundamental force on which the very survival and development of human communities depends. It is the connective tissue that unites individuals in society, a pledge of the survival of culture and the driver of every innovation. Without the possibility of transferring thoughts, experience and knowledge from generation to generation, human survival would remain bound within the limits of instinct, and the concept of culture would be unimaginable.

Figure 1.1: Communication and development of civilization.

The fundamental shift from simple signaling systems, such as we find in the animal world, to the complexity of human language is the result of a long-term evolutionary process. This heritage, made up of a series of cognitive and social adaptations, created the preconditions for the further development of communication and laid the foundations for the entire human culture. It is not manifested in a single ability, but in a complex interweaving of several factors that encouraged and shaped each other.

Figure 1.2: Evolution of human communication – from primates to conventionalized language.

A key moment in this development is the transition from predominantly indexical signs, firmly tied to immediate reality, to the use of symbols. While indexical signs point to something present and correlated (for example, smoke to fire), symbols derive their value from agreements within the community, thereby enabling the discussion of objects, beings and phenomena that are not spatially or temporally present, as well as abstract concepts.

Index sign: A sign whose meaning derives from a causal or correlational connection with an object (e.g. smoke refers to fire); refers to the immediately present and perceived, in contrast to the symbols that arise from convention and allow speaking about the absent and abstract. Symbol: Linguistic or other sign whose meaning does not derive from physical similarity or causal connection with the object, but from social agreement (convention); allows speaking about the absent and abstract, in contrast to the indexical sign that refers to the immediately present.

However, such a transition is only possible with profound changes in the social structure. The development of collaborative behavior, as Tomasello (2008) points out, created an environment in which information sharing became evolutionarily beneficial. In communities where individuals with the characteristics of independent action, agents, depended on each other for survival, the ability to communicate precisely and reliably brought a direct advantage.

Agent: An individual or system that acts in an environment with specific goals; in the context of communication – a participant who can send and receive messages and coordinate their actions with others.

At the core of this collaborative paradigm lies the concept of shared intentionality, i.e. the ability of agents to shape common goals with others and coordinate their actions to achieve them. This cognitive ability enabled joint hunting or defense, but also the understanding that the act of communication is a joint effort of sender and receiver to establish a common reference point. It is inextricably linked with the development of the theory of mind, the ability to attribute mental states - beliefs, desires and intentions - to others, as well as to oneself. Without a theory of mind, the recipient of the message would not be able to understand the speaker’s intention, and complex symbolic communication would be reduced to misunderstanding.

Joint intentionality: The ability to form common goals with others and coordinate actions to achieve them; the basis of collaborative communication. Theory of mind: Cognitive ability to attribute mental states – beliefs, desires, intentions and knowledge – to others and to oneself; key to understanding the speaker’s intention in communication and predicting other people’s behavior. Without theory of mind, complex symbolic communication would not be possible because the recipient of the message would not be able to deduce what the speaker wants to achieve with it.

Nevertheless, the development of communication systems based on trust has inevitably opened up space for manipulation and deception. As soon as communication became a means of influencing the behavior of others, the possibility of its abuse for one’s own benefit also appeared. This prompted a sort of evolutionary arms race (Krebs & Dawkins, 1984) between the ability to deceive and the ability to detect deception. On the one hand, agents developed increasingly sophisticated deception strategies, while, on the other hand, they perfected cognitive mechanisms for recognizing inconsistencies, assessing the reliability of sources, and monitoring the reputation of individuals within the community. This constant tension between cooperation and conflict further encouraged the development of cognitive complexity.

With the increase in the complexity of the messages that had to be conveyed - who did what, what, to whom, when and where - the need for their organization also appeared. It is from this need that grammar grows: a system of rules that enables the combination of a limited number of symbols (words) into an unlimited number of meaningful statements. The development of syntax enabled the precise coding of relationships between participants and actions, which made communication more expressive and unequivocal.

Grammar: A system of rules that allows combining a limited number of language units (words, morphemes) into an unlimited number of meaningful statements; it encompasses syntax, morphology, and related conventions that determine the structure and interpretation of language.

Ultimately, the legacy for the further development of communication is a complex set that includes a social structure based on cooperation and trust, cognitive abilities such as shared intentionality and theory of mind, and a dynamic balance between deception and its detection, which all together created evolutionary pressure for the development of a grammatically organized symbolic system. It is a dynamic foundation on which increasingly complex forms of human interaction, knowledge and culture are built even today.

Figure 1.3: The interconnectedness of social, cognitive, and communication processes—collaborative communication and theory of mind drive development, while the evolutionary race between deception and its detection creates pressure for cognitive complexity and a grammatically structured symbolic system.

Oral tradition, the first and longest-lived communication technology, transformed fleeting memories into living archives. She wove them into the fabric of epics, myths and rituals, transmitting the worldview and identity of the community through the ages with a permanence almost like that of the genetic code. With the invention of writing, words gained material permanence, imprinted in clay, engraved in stone or written on papyrus and paper. Writing enabled an unimaginable accumulation of knowledge, the development of abstract thought, and the construction of complex administrative, legal, and philosophical systems that defined great empires and epochs. Each subsequent technological milestone—from Gutenberg’s printing press that democratized knowledge, to the telegraph and telephone that bridged spatial distances, to radio, television, and finally the Internet that created the contours of a global community—opened a new chapter in the constant evolution of how people exchange meaning with each other.

Figure 1.4: Functions of oral transmission.

The modern age is witnessing a technological breakthrough that, with its depth and reach, surpasses many previous ones. It is about the emergence of large language models (Large Language Model, LLM), advanced artificial intelligence systems such as GPT (OpenAI, 2024b), Claude (Anthropic, 2024), Gemini or Llama models. Built on inconceivably huge corpora of digitized human language and knowledge, these systems are trained to recognize and reproduce the most subtle patterns of human communication. They reveal the fascinating duality elegantly summarized by academic Milena Žic Fuchs (Žic-Fuchs, 1991), distinguishing knowledge about the world (facts, concepts, relationships) and knowledge about language (grammar, stylistics, pragmatics). Today’s great language models master the language code with exceptional skill, creating texts that are grammatically coherent, stylistically adapted, and often factually accurate and contextually appropriate. They mimic human language production with incredible persuasiveness, often reaching, and in some narrowly defined tasks even surpassing, human performance.

LLM – Large Language Model: An artificial intelligence system trained on huge text corpora that predicts the next token (word or part of a word) and generates or completes the text based on it; examples include GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama.

Figure 1.5: Development of active power through literacy.

But large language models cease to be mere text generators the moment they are transformed into communication agents by incorporating them into broader information systems and equipping them with goals, data access tools, and memory mechanisms. Thus, they become our new digital interlocutors, assistants and collaborators - and perhaps true communication partners. Their impact is already evident in the reshaping of the landscape of human interaction: they enable real-time language translation, run service automatons (chatbots) that provide personalized customer support, help scientists analyze complex data sets, assist programmers in writing code, stimulate creative processes, and open new vistas of global collaboration and education. They are increasingly assuming the role of universal translators and mediators of knowledge, capable of bridging linguistic, disciplinary and cultural barriers.

Communication agent: A system based on LLM (or similar language technology) equipped with goals, data access tools, and memory mechanisms, which dialogues with the user and performs tasks; it goes beyond the role of a mere text generator and becomes a participant in the interaction.

Figure 1.6: Historical development of communication to AI-mediated communication.

The central guiding thought of this book is the assertion that large language models, and the communication agents they trigger, do not represent just a new technological tool, a gadget (gadget), but a fundamental transformation of the very nature of communication. Their potential penetrates deeply into the structure of social relations, human cognition and the very essence of what it means to be a human being who communicates in the digital age. Precisely because they carry with them unimagined possibilities, it is of crucial importance to critically penetrate into their inherent capabilities and limitations. It is equally important to shape their development and application ethically, in order to serve the improvement of human dignity and the general betterment. The book is intended as a systematic review of communication technologies, a journey that begins in the deep past and ends with a reasoned look into the possible future of human-machine interaction.

Our journey begins with a detailed overview of the history of communication technologies (Chapter 2), from its origins in oral tradition to the digital revolution. Understanding the ways in which previous technologies - the letter, the press, the telegraph, the radio - shaped social structures and human cognition, provides us with the necessary framework for assessing the depth and direction of the changes brought about by the current artificial intelligence revolution.

After the historical foundations, we dive into the very heart of the technology that powers today’s communication agents: the world of large language models (Chapter 3). We will reveal their anatomy, with a special emphasis on the transformer architecture, and we will follow the entire life cycle of the language model. Each of these stages – from collecting unimaginably large sets of text and image data to pre-training on powerful computer clusters, through fine-tuning for specific tasks and the crucial process of matching with human feedback, all the way to rigorous performance evaluation – will be explained in detail. We will also not ignore the darker side of this technology: its significant limitations, risks of built-in biases, security issues and the enormous consumption of resources required by these digital giants.

With technological understanding as a basis, we enter into a deeper, conceptual breakdown of the relationship between language, society and artificial intelligence (Chapter 4). Here we will deconstruct language as a system of meaning and as a social practice, exploring the ways in which large language models, as new participants in communication, encroach on these processes. We will look at how these systems simulate social interactions, influence our sense of identity and potentially reshape our perception of reality, acting as powerful algorithmic lenses. We will pay special attention to the role of language in the collective creation of knowledge and culture and the new role of communication agents in these processes - from collaboration in scientific research to co-creation in art.

Since it is difficult to talk about artificial intelligence without understanding its material basis, we will explore (Chapter 5) the inextricable link between the exponential growth of processing power and the progress of artificial intelligence, drawing comparisons with the evolution of the human brain. We will consider how this power enables today’s models and what horizons it opens for future, even more powerful systems, including potential multi-agent systems and agent swarms and the long-term quest for artificial general intelligence (AGI).

AGI: General Artificial Intelligence (Artificial General Intelligence) – a hypothetical system that would possess a human level of general intelligence and could solve a wide range of tasks without being limited to one domain; for now the goal is research, not existing technology.

After the theoretical and technological foundations, we move on to the practical construction of communication partners (Chapter 6). This chapter details the journey from the core core of a large language model to a functional and useful AI agent. We will explore key techniques such as prompt engineering (Prompt Engineering), i.e. the art of precise model management, then enriched data retrieval (Retrieval-Augmented Generation, RAG) which enables agents to access external, up-to-date knowledge, and mechanisms for using tools (Tool Use) which give them the ability to act in the digital world.

How do these agents work in practice? Chapter 7 provides concrete examples and case studies, illustrating how they are used to transform customer support, personalize educational processes, improve marketing strategies, and find applications in healthcare, business processes, and creative industries. We will analyze the ways in which they create new value, but also the new challenges they bring with them.

Finally, in the last chapter (Chapter 8), we will venture a speculative but grounded look into the near future (period 2030-2035). Through a narrative sketch of a day in the life and an analysis of key trends such as ambient intelligence, hyperpersonalization and the synergy of agent swarms, we will try to imagine what everyday life permeated by ubiquitous, proactive and autonomous digital companions might look like. We will consider the potential for true human-AI symbiosis, but also the deep social and ethical dilemmas such a future holds, balancing between utopian promises and dystopian risks.

Several central thoughts run through the entire book: the evolution of communication as a continuous but accelerated process; large language models as extremely powerful, but also essentially limited technology; communication agents as entities that go beyond the role of a mere tool and become participants in the interaction; and, finally, the permanent need for critical consideration of ethical consequences and responsible shaping of the present reality and the future. Our journey aims to provide the reader with knowledge of how these systems work, as well as a deeper understanding of why they are important and where they might take us.

Throughout history, communication has been the key mechanism by which we have built bridges between minds, created shared worlds, and shaped the institutions and cultures that define our civilization. Today, at this historic crossroads, large language models and the agents they drive offer us the opportunity – but also the responsibility – to make that mechanism exponentially faster, more globally accessible, and potentially more intelligent than ever before. This book is an invitation to explore that intersection: the place where the thousand-year history of human communication meets the most advanced technology of the 21st century, technology that reshapes our tools, but also asks anew the fundamental question: what does it mean to be a human being who creates his own world through communication?

2 History and evolution of communication technologies

2.1 Communication as the basis and material of civilization

Consideration of the essence of civilization inevitably leads us to its fundamental beginning and material: communication. Civilization can be understood as a dynamic and continuous process of social life, which is entirely enabled, shaped and maintained by communication. Man’s nature as a social being dictates the need for the exchange of thoughts, feelings and experiences, and this exchange, mediated by complex symbolic systems, becomes the foundation on which increasingly complex social structures are built.

Communication is therefore a process by which a shared world of meaning is created and maintained. It is the ability to create and transmit abstract ideas and shared narratives – myths, laws, values and history – that enables the cooperation of a large number of individuals and thus lays the cornerstone of any civilization (Harari, 2011). Without this ability to transcend the immediate, experiential world, human communities would remain limited to small, kinship-related groups. Through language, writing, art and other symbolic forms, thought is materialized; it becomes external and accessible to others, regardless of spatial and temporal distance.

This process of materializing thoughts through communication gives birth to what we call artifacts. Artifacts in this sense do not only refer to material objects such as tools, buildings or works of art, but also include immaterial creations: laws, social norms, scientific theories, philosophical systems and religious doctrines. Each such artifact is an embodiment of knowledge and experience, a frozen communication waiting to be unraveled and reactivated in the minds of new generations. In this way culture acquires its cumulative nature; each generation does not start anew, but interacts with the inherited information environment shaped by its predecessors.

Artifact: In the context of communication and culture – a material or immaterial creation (law, norm, theory, work of art, technology) in which knowledge and experience are preserved; it mediates between agents across time and space and enables the cumulability of culture. Cumulative culture: The property of human culture that knowledge, skills and institutions are gradually upgraded from generation to generation, because through communication and artifacts, previous achievements are preserved on which each new generation can build on its own innovations; a mechanism that makes cultural evolution progressive rather than cyclical (Tomasello, 1999; Henrich, 2016).

Civilization can therefore be understood as a complex and inexhaustible interaction network consisting of agents (human beings) and artifacts. Within that network, communication is the driving force behind all interactions. Agents communicate with each other to coordinate their actions, but they also communicate with artifacts - they read books, interpret laws, use technology, apply scientific knowledge. Artifacts, on the other hand, mediate communication between agents, often across vast temporal and spatial ranges, and thus shape their thinking and actions (Floridi, 2014).

Figure 2.1: Schematic representation of the relationship between agents, communication and artifacts as the basis of cumulative culture.

Communication is the material and fabric of civilization itself. It is the process by which abstract ideas can be transformed into permanent artifacts, by which knowledge is transmitted and multiplied, and by which individual agents are connected into a complex, self-sustaining whole that we call civilization. Observing the history of civilization means following the traces of this continuous communication - from the first oral traditions and paintings in caves to today’s global digital networks. In every form, communication remains a fundamental prerequisite and an inexhaustible source of human creativity.

2.2 Oral tradition and living archives

The term oral tradition encompasses a complex process that cannot be reduced to mere memory or simple storage of information about the past. On the contrary, it is an active act of transmitting, shaping and constantly reviving cultural knowledge.

Oral transmission: Way of transmitting knowledge, narrative and culture through speech and memory, without writing; knowledge lives in carriers (living archives) and changes in every performance; basic communication technology before the advent of writing. Cultures based on orality have a fundamentally different attitude towards the past than those based on writing; in them, the past is not a fixed and unchanging whole, but a fluid and adaptable reality that is reaffirmed in every act of storytelling (Ong, 1982). This reality is not preserved in dead letters, but in living people.

The bearers of such tradition can rightly be called living archives. However, this name does not imply that they are only passive containers of information, similar to shelves in a library.

Living archive: Bearer of oral tradition who actively interprets, adapts and transmits cultural knowledge; knowledge is embodied in voice, gesture and memory, not in written record; each performance is unique. Their role is active and creative. A living archive interprets, adapts and transmits inherited knowledge, imbuing it with its own experience and understanding of the world. Each of his performances, whether it is a song, a story or a ritual formula, is a unique and unrepeatable act of creation, and not a mere reproduction of an existing template (Lord, 2000).

In this process, the agent, that is, the bearer and performer of the tradition, is a key figure who actively shapes the narrative. His role goes beyond the function of a transmitter because through his performance he confirms, and sometimes reshapes, the values and knowledge of the community. The knowledge that the living archive possesses is not abstract, but deeply embodied. It resides in his or her voice, rhythm of speech, gesticulation and memory of the body, making the whole of the performer and the performance inseparable.

The difference between oral and written archives is therefore fundamental. By its very nature, the written archive tends towards staticity, immutability and apparent objectivity, separating knowledge from its human source. On the other hand, the oral archive is inextricably linked to the person of the performer and the social context. It is dynamic, changeable and necessarily imbued with subjectivity, because its meaning is constituted precisely in the living relationship between the narrator, the listener and the moment of performance (Goody & Watt, 1968).

This gives the oral tradition an exceptional social function. It is a cohesive force that creates and sustains a community, providing it with a sense of continuity and belonging through a shared repertoire of stories, beliefs and memories. This is why the content of the delivery is never more important than the context of its performance. Circumstances about the identity of the speaker, to whom he addresses, when and on what occasion he speaks, are an integral part of the message being transmitted. In modern times, we are faced with the paradox of the technological record of oral tradition. While recording enables its preservation in the face of the threat of oblivion, it simultaneously fixes and deadens what is essentially alive, fluid and performative. Such a record, although necessary for the preservation of the artifacts themselves, is only a faint reflection of the completeness of the event of oral creation.

2.2.1 The complexity of the oral tradition

The approach to oral tradition is often burdened by a simplified view that reduces it to a mere transmission of unchanging contents from generation to generation, almost as a kind of mechanical memorization of a static repertoire of stories or songs. However, such an understanding ignores its inherent layering and dynamism of living and complex systems of communication, knowledge and art, the nature of which cannot be exhausted by one-sided explanations. Oral traditions represent complete cognitive and social worlds, woven into the very fabric of the community that creates, transmits and constantly reshapes them.

The central element of this complexity is the fact that the oral tradition is not realized in a fixed, written text but in the performance event. Each performance represents a unique act of creation in which the agent, that is, the performer (singer, storyteller), does not mechanically reproduce a memorized template, but actively composes it at the moment of presentation (Lord, 1960). In doing so, he makes use of the rich heritage of traditional tools: established formulas, metric patterns, typical scenes and thematic sets. These elements function as building blocks that enable improvisation within the given stylistic and content frameworks. The agent is a co-creator who adapts the tradition to the specific context, audience and own inspiration.

Furthermore, the complexity of the oral tradition is manifested in its multimodality. It is rarely reduced exclusively to the verbal component. Sound, rhythm, melody, gestures, facial expressions and the entire physicality of the performer are inextricably intertwined with the spoken or sung word. The meaning is conveyed by the semantics of the sentences, but also by the way they are delivered - by intonation, pauses, accents and emotional charge. The role of the audience is not passive; with her reactions, incentives or silence, she directly participates in shaping the performance, creating a dynamic feedback loop with the performer. Performance is therefore always a dialogic and social act, deeply conditioned by the situation in which it occurs.

Multimodality: Simultaneous use and interweaving of multiple communication channels – speech, gesture, mimicry, intonation, rhythm, music and spatial relationship – in order to convey meaning; in the oral tradition it means the inseparability of the verbal and physical dimensions of performance, while in modern digital communication it includes text, image, sound and video as integrated components of the message.

Finally, a fundamental feature of oral tradition is the creative tension between permanence and changeability. In order to survive, a tradition must possess a sufficient measure of stability that ensures its recognition and continuity through generations. At the same time, in order to remain alive and relevant, it must constantly adapt and change with each new performance. This apparent paradox is resolved in the understanding that traditionality does not lie in the immutability of words, but in the deeper structures and meaning potentials they evoke. Each formula or theme carries with it a wealth of associations and references to the entire tradition, creating what John Miles Foley (1991) calls traditional referentiality. Words in oral performance have a far greater semantic charge because they echo the unspoken but present context of the entire traditional knowledge. Because of all of the above, the oral tradition should be viewed as an intricate ecosystem in which the cognitive processes of memory and creation, the social dynamics of performance, and the aesthetic values of language, music, and movement merge into a unique and unrepeatable human experience.

Figure 2.2: Dynamic system of oral tradition – tradition, performer, performance and audience in the cycle of transmission and renewal of knowledge.

2.2.2 Collective imagination and identity

The foundation of human culture and, consequently, collective identity rests on the unique cognitive ability of humans for common intentionality – the ability to create and share complex social realities that exist exclusively in the domain of collective imagination. It is this ability, as pointed out by researchers such as Tomasello (2014) and Harari (2014), that distinguishes human culture from the rudimentary forms of social learning present in other primates. While animal communities are based on direct interaction and genetically determined behaviors, human societies are built on shared beliefs in concepts such as nations, money, laws, or human rights, which have no tangible existence outside of shared agreement and imagination. The most obvious and powerful example of such an imagined reality is the nation, which Benedict Anderson (1983) precisely defined as an imagined community. Members of one nation will never know each other, but in their minds there is a vivid idea of community. This sense of belonging does not come from direct contact, but is nourished and maintained through shared symbols such as flags and anthems, collective rituals such as national holidays, and narratives about shared origins, history and destiny. Through these mechanisms, a deep emotional bond is created that connects millions of strangers into a coherent whole. In the modern world, the reach and forms of the collective imagination have been significantly expanded by the action of the global media. In his analysis of global cultural flows, Arjun Appadurai (1996) introduces the concepts of mediascapes and ideoscapes. These landscapes, made up of images, narratives and ideas that circulate through the media, enable the creation of identities that transcend traditional national boundaries. Individuals today can develop a sense of belonging to global subcultures, social movements or diasporic communities, thus confirming that the collective imagination is not limited exclusively to the territory of the nation-state. However, it is important to emphasize that the collective imagination also has a distinct material dimension. Imagined realities are embodied and made permanent through monuments, architecture, flags, legal documents and social institutions. These material objects and structures act as anchors of collective identity, giving abstract ideas a concrete and visible form (Latour, 2005). The monument to the unknown hero is not only a stone but also a materialized narrative of sacrifice and national pride; the constitution is not only a piece of paper but also a tangible promise of common rights and order. At the same time, the field of collective imagination is dynamic and fraught with conflicts. Different social groups are constantly competing to impose their own vision of reality and define dominant narratives about who “we” are. Identity is therefore not a static and predetermined category, but, as Judith Butler (Butler and Trouble 1990) shows in the context of gender, is the result of a continuous process of negotiation, contestation and performative repetition. History is filled with struggles over the interpretation of the past, the meaning of national symbols or the definition of community boundaries, which testifies to the fact that collective identity is always an open arena of power. In this complex power relationship, the individual agent actively participates in the process of creating meaning - he interprets, accepts, adapts, but also resists or reshapes collective ideas. At this intersection of individual action and collective structures, the real life of identity takes place. Through the action of the agent, the dominant imagination can be further strengthened and confirmed, but it can also be contested, undermined and finally changed, thereby opening up space for the creation of new forms of collective existence.

Figure 2.3: The process of collective identity formation: from collective imagination and shared beliefs to social order and collective identity (feedback).

2.2.3 Social functions of oral tradition

To view the oral tradition exclusively as a treasury of antiquities or a mere repository of aesthetically shaped texts would be to overlook its fundamental purpose and dynamic role in community life. Its existence is certainly conditioned by the individual need for artistic expression, but above all by its deep and multi-layered rootedness in social reality. Oral traditions, in all their forms - from myths and epics to proverbs and songs - act as key mechanisms through which a community designs, maintains and transmits its entire worldview and social structure. They become an active agent in its shaping. One of the most important roles of oral tradition is the preservation and transmission of collective memory. In cultures that primarily rely on orality, the stories about the origin of the community, about the deeds of the ancestors, about mythical events and historical milestones form the living fabric of historical consciousness. As a narrative framework that gives meaning and legitimacy to the present, oral tradition connects the community to its origins and ensures a sense of continuity through generations, and establishes and maintains a common identity, because belonging to a community means sharing and knowing its stories.

Collective memory: A socially conditioned and jointly maintained system of memory by which the group preserves, interprets and transmits selected ideas about its own past; in the oral tradition, it is realized through repeated narrative performances (myths, genealogies, epic poems) that give meaning and legitimacy to the present and ensure a sense of continuity and belonging across generations (Halbwachs, 1950; Assmann, 2011).

Furthermore, oral tradition is a fundamental means of education and socialization. Through short stories, fairy tales, riddles and songs, the young generations adopt primarily the language and aesthetic patterns of their culture, but also ethical codes, social norms, rules of conduct and practical knowledge necessary for survival. Instructive stories warn of the consequences of transgression, while heroic poems offer models of desirable action. Thus, tradition acts as an informal but extremely effective educational system that shapes an individual into a full-fledged and functional member of society.

Socialization: The process by which an individual, in interaction with other members of the community, adopts the language, values, norms, knowledge and patterns of behavior necessary for functioning within a certain culture; in oral societies, this process takes place predominantly through narrative and performance forms (stories, fairy tales, riddles, songs) that simultaneously teach, entertain and shape personal and social identity (Berger and Luckmann, 1966).

Oral traditions also have a distinct pragmatic and legal-legitimation function. Myths about the creation of the world or the origin of tribes often serve as charters that confirm and justify existing social order, property relations, political hierarchy, or ritual practices (Finnegan, 1977). Genealogies that are remembered and publicly recited legitimize the right of ruling lineages to power, while oral traditions about court precedents can have the force of unwritten law. Oral tradition thus provides the basis for social stability, offering a supernatural or historical sanction for secular institutions.

Pragmatic function of oral tradition: The role of oral traditions in the direct regulation of social life - from the legal legitimation of government and property relations (through genealogies and myths of origin) to the transfer of practical knowledge and skills necessary for daily survival; tradition acts as an unwritten law and operational manual of the community (Finnegan, 1977; Malinowski, 1926).

The fun and aesthetic function, which is inseparable from all the others, should not be neglected either. Oral performances provide aesthetic pleasure and entertainment, gathering the community in moments of rest and celebration. The skill of the storyteller, singer, or reciter—their ability to master voice, gesture, and interaction with the audience—is critical to the success of message transmission (Bauman, 1986). It is precisely through the artistic dimension of the performance that the content of the tradition becomes attractive, memorable and emotionally effective.

Aesthetic function: The dimension of the communication act in which the form of the message – rhythm, melody, figure, style, narrative structure – becomes a source of pleasure and meaning in itself; in the oral tradition, the aesthetic function is not just a decoration, but a key mechanism that makes the content memorable, emotionally effective and suitable for repeated performance, thus directly ensuring the transmission of culture (Jakobson, 1960; Bauman, 1986).

Finally, oral tradition can also serve as a form of social criticism and commentary, and even as a covert vent for expressing dissent. Through satirical songs, anecdotes about powerful people or allegorical stories about animals, the community can criticize injustice, mock authority or question ruling norms in a way that is often too risky in direct communication. Thus, tradition shows its adaptability and ability to serve not only the maintenance, but also the questioning and subtle change of the social order.

Social criticism in the oral tradition: The function of the oral tradition that allows the community to question, comment on and challenge the existing power relations and social norms through indirect narrative forms – satire, allegory, parody, anecdotes about the powerful and animal fables; since criticism comes in an aesthetically shaped and collectively sanctioned form, it bypasses open conflict while simultaneously opening up space for reconsideration and gradual change of order (Scott, 1990; Finnegan, 1977).

All the mentioned functions – from preservation of memory and education to identification and entertainment – are intertwined and can rarely be viewed separately. Each individual oral performance simultaneously activates several of these roles, confirming that oral tradition is a complete social phenomenon, necessary for the survival and cohesion of the community that creates and nurtures it.

2.3 Literacy as a window into complex knowledge systems

Observing literacy exclusively as the skill of reading and writing means overlooking its deep, transformative role in shaping human thought and the entire social reality. Literacy should be understood as a fundamental technology that changes the cognitive architecture of the individual and opens access to complex, cumulative systems of knowledge, unimaginable in exclusively oral cultures. It is an epistemological prerequisite for the emergence of science, philosophy, law and history in their modern form. The main dividing line that literacy establishes in relation to oral tradition is its ability to externalize and fix thoughts. While the spoken word is inherently transitory and tied to the immediate context of interaction, the written text exists as an autonomous and permanent object, separate from the author and the moment of creation. This durability enables new cognitive operations: re-reading, careful analysis, comparison of different statements created in different times and places, and systematic criticism (Goody & Watt, 1963). The text thereby establishes itself as an external, objectified memory, freeing the mind from the cognitive burden of remembering the entire cultural heritage and allowing it to devote itself to abstract and analytical thinking.

Externalization of thinking: The process of transferring internal cognitive content - ideas, knowledge, reasoning - to an external, permanent and author-independent carrier (written text, diagram, record, digital document); thus, the mind is relieved of the burden of memory, and thought becomes available for re-reading, analysis, criticism and cumulative upgrading through generations, thus opening the prerequisites for the emergence of complex systems of knowledge (Goody, 1977; Donald, 1991; Clark and Chalmers, 1998).

This change profoundly reshapes internal mental processes as well. Mastery of writing encourages the development of linear, sequential thinking, as opposed to the associative and episodic nature of memory in oral cultures. The ability to follow complex syntax, classify information into categories and subcategories, and develop abstract concepts is a direct consequence of long-term exposure to the written word. In addition to storing knowledge, literacy literally restructures neural pathways in the brain, creating prerequisites for new forms of intelligence and introspection (Dehaene, 2009). It is on these cognitive foundations that complex systems of knowledge grow. Science, for example, rests on the possibility of verifying and upgrading previously recorded knowledge; legal systems depend on the precision and immutability of written laws; and philosophical and theological discourses develop through centuries of written debates about the foundational texts. These systems have an internal logic, hierarchy, and cumulative nature, which would be impossible to maintain solely through word of mouth. Written culture creates a vast, intertextual network into which every new knowledge must fit, to which it must refer and which gives it additional meaning. In this complex universe of knowledge, a literate individual becomes an agent - an employee who, through literacy, acquires the means to understand existing systems, as well as to actively participate in them. He can interpret, question, challenge and, finally, contribute to the body of knowledge. Through the act of reading, the agent enters into a dialogue with thinkers from the past, and through the act of writing, he articulates his own knowledge and directs it to future generations (Ong, 1982).

Figure 2.4: The roles of literacy in enabling the agent to access complex knowledge systems and in stimulating cognitive and social transformation.

2.3.1 Different paths to the letter

The appearance of writing in human history can be understood as a layered process that took place in different ways, at different times and prompted by different needs. Historical and archeological findings bear witness to at least four independent, spontaneous centers of literacy: in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Central America. Each of these systems emerged from specific cultural and social circumstances, but the paths that letters and literacy moved on branched off into several fundamental directions. The fundamental difference that emerges in the study of the history of letters is that between the original invention, i.e. the creation of letters de novo, and the process of borrowing or adapting an already existing system. The creation of a letter from the ground up is an extremely rare historical phenomenon, related to the mentioned origins. Much more common is the path of adaptation, where one culture takes a script from another and modifies it to fit the structure of its language. It is a paradigmatic example of the Greek takeover of the Phoenician consonant letter (abjada). The Greeks, faced with a script that did not record the vowels crucial to the phonology of their Indo-European language, repurposed graphemes for the Semitic gutturals they did not need and assigned them the value of vowels. This only resulted in the transmission of an essential structural change that resulted in the first complete alphabet. Similar processes of adaptation have occurred countless times in history, each time confirming that the script is a dynamic system that must adapt to the phonological, morphological and syntactic features of the language it serves. Furthermore, the path to a well-formed writing system can also be viewed through the prism of the way it was created, which can be gradual and emergent, or conscious and engineered. The emergent or organic path implies a long-term, often century-long development, during which the alphabet gradually develops from simpler protosystems, such as pictograms, ideograms or systems for recording numbers and goods. The most famous example is the Sumerian cuneiform script, which evolved from a system of clay tokens used for administrative and economic purposes millennia before the appearance of real writing (Schmandt-Besserat, 1996). This development was a response to the growing needs of a complex society for accurate records. In such a model, the letter appears as the result of a collective and unconscious process, without a named inventor or a precise moment of creation.

Figure 2.5: Development paths of the alphabet (from pictograph to alphabet).

The engineered or deliberate path is the opposite. Here, writing is the result of a conscious and deliberate act of creation undertaken by an individual or a small group. Such an agent acts with a clear goal - to create a script for a specific language, often for cultural, political or religious reasons. The most obvious example of such an endeavor is the Korean script Hangul, which was devised in the 15th century by King Sejong the Great and his scholars to increase literacy and strengthen Korean cultural identity. Hangul was not created by adapting an existing script, but was designed based on phonological analysis of the Korean language, making it one of the most scientifically sound scripts in the world. Similar, although less well-known, examples are the Cherokee language script created in the 19th century by Sequoyah or the numerous scripts designed by Christian missionaries for previously unwritten languages (Cromer, 1997). These two dichotomies – de novo versus adaptation and emergent versus engineering – are not always strictly separate and can be intertwined. The adaptation of an existing script can also be the result of a deliberate act, such as contemporary orthographic reforms, or it can occur gradually and organically over centuries of use.

Figure 2.6: Development of active power through literacy: from basic literacy (reading and writing) through text comprehension and recognition of system rules to literacy in complex systems (legal, digital) and effective agent action.

Understanding these different paths is crucial because it shows that there is no single “evolution” of writing that necessarily leads from pictorial to alphabetic. Each writing system is a reflection of the history, culture and linguistic structure of the community that uses it. The life of the letter is inseparably connected with the life of that community, and the ways in which it develops and spreads are as diverse as human societies themselves.

2.3.2 Social elite and slow expansion

In the complex fabric of social relations, the social elite occupies a dual and sometimes contradictory role in the processes of innovation diffusion. Although history has recorded elites as the first adopters of certain innovations, especially those that strengthen their status, their position in the power structure often makes them a key factor in slowing down or even stopping diffusion processes. This phenomenon often results from active action aimed at preserving the existing order (status quo). The fundamental cause of such action lies in the fact that every major innovation, whether technological, cultural or social in nature, has the potential to redistribute power, influence and resources within the community. The social elite, by definition, benefits the most from the existing situation. Their power and privileged position are directly linked to existing norms, values and material relations. Therefore, any innovation that could disturb this balance is perceived as a threat. Preservation of their own interests thus becomes the driving force of resistance to changes that come from outside their controlled circles.

Redistribution of power: A change in the distribution of influence, resources and authority among actors within the social structure, which occurs when a new technology, practice or idea changes the previous channels of access to knowledge, communication or material means; in the context of communication innovations (letters, press, internet) the redistribution of power means the process by which previously excluded groups gain the ability to act, while the previous elites lose their monopoly over information and interpretation of reality (Castells, 2009; Eisenstein, 1979).

Furthermore, social stratification itself creates barriers to expansion. Social elites are often characterized by a high degree of homophily - a tendency to associate and interact with individuals who are similar in education, background and status. Such confinement to one’s own social networks significantly limits the flow of information and influence between the elite and the wider population. Communication channels become interrupted or one-way, and the elite acts as a kind of “gatekeeper”, filtering which ideas and practices will reach the rest of society. As Rogers (2003) states, when elites adopt an innovation exclusively for themselves to emphasize their special status, they actually prevent its further diffusion, instead of encouraging it.

Social stratification: Hierarchical stratification of society into levels (layers, classes, estates) that differ in access to material resources, education, power and prestige; in the context of communication technologies, stratification determines who first adopts an innovation, who has access to information and who acts as a gatekeeper that accelerates or slows down the spread of new ideas and practices to other parts of society (Weber, 1922; Bourdieu, 1984; Rogers, 2003).

The role of a change agent in such a context is extremely difficult. If the agent does not belong to the elite or does not have direct access to its members, his messages will have difficulty overcoming social and cultural distance. The elite may reject an innovation not so much because of its intrinsic properties as because of the origin of its bearer. News that comes from “below” or from the outside can be perceived as vulgar, inappropriate or threatening, thereby discrediting its symbolic value in advance. This establishes a mechanism in which the elite not only slows down change, but actively works to delegitimize innovations that do not serve to strengthen its position.

Cultural distance: Degree of difference in values, norms, language, education and life experiences between two social groups; the greater the cultural distance between the bearer of the innovation and potential recipients, the more difficult is the transfer of ideas and practices, because the message loses credibility or is reinterpreted through the prism of the recipient’s own symbolic framework (Rogers, 2003; Hofstede, 2001).

Figure 2.7: A model of slowing diffusion through the social elite: the elite acts as a filter that accepts the innovation and accelerates its spread if it is aligned with its interests (benefit, status, power), or rejects it and slows down its spread if it represents a threat to the existing order.

2.4 The printing press: a turning point in the spread of ideas

The invention of the movable type printing press, which is attributed to Johannes Gutenberg around 1450, represents one of the most significant technological and cultural breakthroughs in human history. Before Gutenberg, knowledge was transmitted and preserved in the form of manuscripts, the creation of which was a long, painstaking and extremely expensive process, mostly limited to monastery scriptoriums and court workshops. Each copy was unique, and its creation could take months, even years, which made the book a rare and precious object available only to a small elite. The limited number of copies and the high price significantly slowed down and narrowed the flow of information and ideas. Gutenberg’s invention fundamentally transformed the material reality of the book and thereby triggered an avalanche of social, religious and scientific changes. By combining the technology of movable metal letters, a press adapted from winemaking, and newly developed oil-based printing ink, a system was created that enabled fast, cheap and mass production of texts. While the monk-copyist wrote a single manuscript, the printing press could now reproduce hundreds and thousands of identical copies. This change in the scale of production necessarily led to a drastic drop in price, with which the written word began its journey towards wider layers of society, gradually leaving the exclusive space of church and noble libraries. The consequences of that technological revolution were far-reaching and profound. The printing press became a key agent in spreading the ideas of the Reformation. The ability to quickly print and distribute writings, such as Martin Luther’s 95 Theses, allowed criticism of church practices to spread across Europe at a speed previously unimaginable. This broke the monopoly of the Catholic Church over the interpretation of holy scriptures and religious doctrines. The printing of the Bible in the vernacular languages further strengthened this process, allowing individuals direct access to the text, which until then had been mediated exclusively by the clergy in the Latin language. In the field of science, the press enabled what is today considered the basis of scientific progress: the reliable and wide dissemination of knowledge. Scientists could more easily share their discoveries, and the accuracy of printed texts and diagrams, as opposed to manuscripts subject to copying errors, provided a solid foundation for further research. As Elizabeth Eisenstein (1979) points out in her capital work, this “fixity of print” created the preconditions for the cumulative growth of knowledge and the scientific revolution that followed in the following centuries. The ideas of Copernicus, Galileo or Newton could circulate among scholars across Europe, encouraging debate, verification and improvement.

Dissemination of knowledge: Systematic dissemination of knowledge, ideas and information from the source to a wider circle of recipients through communication channels (manuscript, print, digital network); is a key assumption of cumulative culture because it allows discoveries to become available for verification, critique, and upgrade by other agents, thus transforming knowledge from an individual achievement into a common good that accelerates further progress (Eisenstein, 1979; Rogers, 2003).

Figure 2.8: The impact of the printing press on the spread of knowledge and social changes: from Gutenberg’s invention (c. 1440) and the mass production of written materials to the increased availability of books, the spread of literacy and ideas (humanism, the Renaissance, the Reformation), the standardization of language and the emergence of the public sphere and public opinion.

Furthermore, the press played a crucial role in the formation of modern nations and the standardization of vernacular languages. Printers, in search of a wider market, chose and promoted certain dialects, which, thanks to the mass distribution of printed works, gradually imposed themselves as the language standard. This created the basis for linguistic and cultural unity in wider areas, which was one of the cornerstones in the process of creating national identities. Viewed in this light, the printing press is an active agent of change which, according to the insights of Marshall McLuhan (1962), reshaped human sensorium and cognitive processes. By emphasizing the visual over the auditory, the press encouraged the development of a linear, sequential and analytical way of thinking, which became a feature of Western civilization in the period known as “Gutenberg’s Galaxy”. The influence of the printing press is therefore not exhausted in technical innovation; he reshaped the ways in which people think, communicate and organize their societies, laying the foundations for the emergence of the modern world.

Figure 2.9: The printing press as an agent of cognitive change - McLuhan’s “Gutenberg’s galaxy”: from emphasizing the visual over the auditory through linear, sequential thinking to the analytical way of processing information.

2.4.1 Mass production and democratization of knowledge

The appearance of mass production of books, made possible by Gutenberg’s invention of the movable type printing press in the middle of the 15th century, should be considered a turning point in the history of Western civilization. Until that time, knowledge contained in books was confined within narrow circles. Books were rare and precious items, multiplied by painstaking work of copyists in monastery scriptoriums, which made them available almost exclusively to the priestly and noble elite. The printing press fundamentally changed that order, enabling the rapid and significantly cheaper production of printed materials and creating the prerequisites for a more extensive spread of literacy among the wider strata of the population. This transformation was particularly clearly manifested during the Protestant Reformation. Martin Luther, recognizing the power of the new media, used the press for the mass dissemination of his writings, thereby inciting religious and social changes of unprecedented proportions. Equally, the press served as a powerful stimulus for the development of science. It enabled scholars to exchange knowledge and discoveries with a previously unimaginable speed, which laid the foundations for the scientific revolution and the establishment of a systematic scientific discourse (Eisenstein, 1979). A kind of Res publica litterarum was created, a community of scholars all over Europe connected by the printed word, who could discuss, build on and check the works of their contemporaries. This entire process is rightly called the democratization of knowledge. However, this term does not mean only easy access to existing information. Its meaning is deeper and includes the gradual empowerment of individuals for active participation in the creation, verification and dissemination of new knowledge. Knowledge thus ceases to be the exclusive property of privileged groups and becomes a common good, subject to public discussion and criticism.

Democratization of knowledge: Gradual removal of social, economic and institutional obstacles to access to information and knowledge, which gives an ever-widening circle of agents the ability not only to receive but also to create, verify and disseminate knowledge; historically initiated by the invention of printing, and nowadays accelerated by digital technology and open access, the democratization of knowledge transforms it from the privilege of the few into a common good subject to public discussion and criticism (Eisenstein, 1979; Castells, 2010).

Figure 2.10: The path of knowledge from limited access in manuscript culture to wider availability through the printing revolution, culminating in the democratization of knowledge.

It should, of course, be noted that this transition was neither immediate nor without resistance; it took centuries for the effects of the printing revolution to fully manifest and permeate every pore of society. In today’s time, with the advent of digital technology and the Internet, a transformation of comparable, if not greater, proportions is taking place. The Internet can be seen as a contemporary counterpart to the printing press, which accelerates and expands the process of democratization of knowledge to a global level, bringing with it new opportunities, but also new challenges.

2.4.2 Reformation and scientific revolution

The period of the 16th and 17th centuries in European history was marked by two profound and transformative movements: the Reformation and the Scientific Revolution. Their simultaneity, as well as their partial geographical overlap, encourage consideration of complex connections and mutual influences. Although a simple cause-and-effect relationship cannot be established, it is clear that the Reformation created an intellectual, social and cultural atmosphere that favored the emergence and development of modern science. The invention of the printing press played a key role in the spread of reformation ideas, but also in creating the basis for scientific progress. By enabling the mass and rapid reproduction of texts, the press undermined the Catholic Church’s monopoly over the knowledge and interpretation of scriptures. The principle of sola scriptura, one of the central pillars of the Reformation, encouraged believers to independently read and reflect on the Bible, which consequently led to an increase in literacy. This newly acquired skill and habit of critical reading was not limited exclusively to religious texts, but also spread to other areas of human knowledge, including scientific ones. The availability of printed works enabled a faster and wider exchange of ideas among scholars across Europe, creating the foundations for the scholarly community as we know it today. In its essence, the Reformation represented a fundamental challenge to the spiritual and secular authority of the Catholic Church. Martin Luther’s act, which publicly questioned the infallibility of the pope and church councils, resonated far beyond theological circles. This undermining of a monolithic authority created an intellectual atmosphere in which it became conceivable, and even desirable, to question other established dogmas, including scientific ones, such as the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic geocentric system, which the Church accepted. If the authority of the Church could be questioned in the field of faith, why could it not be questioned in the field of interpretation of nature? In this way, the Reformation, albeit unintentionally, contributed to the secularization of knowledge and made critical questioning legitimate as a valid cognitive method. The Protestant doctrine of the “priesthood of all believers”, which gives each individual the right and duty to independently interpret God’s word, finds its scientific analogy. The scientist, as an individual agent, now assumes the role of one who directly “reads” and interprets the “book of nature”, without the mediation of ancient authorities such as Aristotle or Galen. This new epistemological paradigm, which emphasized personal experience and interpretation, was not limited to theology. It was also transferred to the study of nature, which began to be perceived as “God’s second book” (Harrison, 2007), open to reading and interpretation through observation and experiment. In his famous thesis, Max Weber connected Protestant ethics with the spirit of capitalism, and Robert K. Merton established a similar connection between Puritanism, as one of the branches of Protestantism, and the development of experimental science in England in the 17th century (Merton, 1970). According to Merton, Puritan values such as diligence, methodology, and utilitarianism encouraged scientific research that could bring practical benefit and glorify God through the discovery of the laws of his creation.

Figure 2.11: Schematic representation of the key consequences of the Reformation that contributed to the creation of an enabling environment for the scientific revolution: Reformation incentives, reinforced by printing technology, lead to the fragmentation of authority and the emphasis on individual knowledge, which creates fertile ground for new scientific methods and discoveries.

However, it should be emphasized that the relationship between the Reformation and science was not uniquely encouraging. The reformers themselves, including Luther and Calvin, expressed considerable skepticism and even open opposition to some new scientific ideas, such as Copernicus’ heliocentric theory. Their primary goal was the restoration of faith, not the promotion of science. Furthermore, the Scientific Revolution was not an exclusively Protestant phenomenon; scientists like Copernicus, Galileo and Descartes worked within the Catholic world. Therefore, the impact of the Reformation on science is not so much manifested in direct doctrinal support as in its indirect and often unintentional consequences: the fragmentation of intellectual authority, the promotion of literacy and the culture of reading, and the establishment of a new value system in which the individual agent, either as a believer or as a scientist, became the center of the cognitive process.

Figure 2.12: The complex relationship between the Reformation and science – the stimulating and limiting effects of the Reformation and the Catholic contribution to the scientific revolution.

2.5 Telegraph and telephone: The beginning of electronic communication

The nineteenth century brought a fundamental change in the history of human communication by introducing technologies that for the first time enabled the transmission of messages at a speed greater than any physical vehicle. This marked the beginning of the era of electronic communication, the foundations of which are still felt today in all modern networks.

Figure 2.13: Schematic representation of the transition to the age of electronic communication: from the transmission of messages faster than physical transport to the telegraph, the telephone and changes in social organization.

2.5.1 Telegraph: new speeds and new horizons

The electric telegraph profoundly and permanently altered the contours of human communication, establishing a new paradigm that ended the millennia-old dependence of information transmission on the physical speed of the messenger, whether by horseman, stagecoach, or ship. Before the telegraph, the world moved at the speed of muscle and wind. After him, the message could threaten the movement of the Sun from east to west, and the distance became a magnitude that, for the first time in history, could be overcome almost instantly. The basic principle of the telegraph was based on a simple but ingenious idea: the conversion of electrical impulses, sent through a long metal wire, into coded characters. Morse code, with its system of dots and dashes, became the lingua franca of that new age, the abstract language of machines that human operators, skilled agents of mediation, turned into meaningful words. This new speed was astonishing. News that would have taken weeks to travel across the Atlantic now reached its destination in minutes. This quantitative change - the drastic reduction of the time required for communication - necessarily stimulated profound qualitative changes in the organization of society. By accelerating existing communication practices, the telegraph created a qualitative leap that gave birth to completely new forms of social and economic interaction. New horizons of possibilities that were previously unimaginable have opened up. Capital and commodity markets, such as those in London and New York, could operate as a single, synchronized system as prices and transactions became instantly available on both sides of the ocean. The business empire could be coordinated from a single center, and armies were given the possibility of centralized command in real time. News agencies, such as Reuters and the Associated Press, grew up precisely on the telegraph network, creating a global flow of news and reshaping public opinion (Standage, 1998). This changed the very perception of space and time; the world began to seem smaller, more connected and busier. To view the telegraph exclusively as a technological artifact would be to ignore its role as the cornerstone of the new communication order. It was a complex socio-technical system that included devices and wires, but also international standards, protocols for sending messages and a whole new profession - telegraph operators. These skilled operators, as key human agents in the communication chain, were an indispensable part of the functioning of the entire network. Their ability to quickly and accurately encode and decode messages was as important as the correctness of the technical facilities themselves. The entire process can be presented as a sequence of steps in which each element has its own irreplaceable role. The laying of the first transatlantic telegraph cable in 1866 was a feat comparable to later space exploration – a triumph of human perseverance and engineering skill. This act symbolically, but also realistically, created a unique information space that encompassed the Old and New Worlds. The telegraph thus laid the foundations for all future forms of electronic communication, from telephone and radio to the Internet. It was the first technology to separate communication from transport, proving that a message can move independently of the physical transfer of objects or people (Carey, 1989). In this sense, the telegraph network of the nineteenth century was not only a predecessor, but an archetype of today’s global information society, and its echoes still shape the way we live, work and understand the world around us.

Figure 2.14: Schematic representation of the significance of the laying of the transatlantic telegraph cable in 1866: a technological undertaking that connected the Old and New worlds and opened up a unique information space.

2.5.2 Telephone: an intimate revolution on the wire

The appearance of the telephone, a technical miracle at the end of the nineteenth century, initiated a further radical transformation of social relations and the very perception of space and time. While the telegraph had already made the world smaller by transmitting coded messages over vast distances, its reach remained in the official, commercial and military spheres. Communication was mediated, asynchronous and devoid of human voice. The telephone, in contrast, returned the most personal thing to the act of communication - the living word, with its color, emphasis, pauses and all those ineffable nuances that reflect human communication. This was the beginning of a quiet but deep revolution that did not take place in the squares or in the parliaments, but in the privacy of homes, on the invisible “wire” that connected the two interlocutors. The key change introduced by the telephone was the abolition of the necessity of physical presence for immediate and intimate communication. Spatial distance, previously an insurmountable obstacle for maintaining close ties, suddenly became surmountable. The human voice, as a carrier of identity and emotions, traveled for kilometers, creating the illusion of proximity and establishing a unique acoustic space shared by only two interlocutors. In this newly created virtual space, one could whisper, console, argue and confide secrets, making the phone a powerful agent in maintaining family and friendship ties that would otherwise weaken under the burden of geographic separation (Fischer, 1992). The new possibility had far-reaching consequences for the structure of everyday life. In the business world, the telephone accelerated decision-making and the flow of information, but its deepest mark remained in the private sphere. For women, who at that time were often spatially limited to the household, the telephone represented a window to the world. It enabled them to build and maintain their own social networks independently of male family members, organize social events and manage the household in a more efficient way. It became a tool of socialization, but also a symbol of a certain social status. The sound of the telephone ringing in the home has become a sign of connection with the outside world. However, this connection also had its other side. The immediacy offered by the telephone also meant the possibility of an unannounced intrusion into the privacy of the home. The ringing of the telephone has become a command that demands immediate attention, interrupting family meals, conversations or moments of rest. The border between public and private, once firmly defined by the doorstep, has become permeable. The disembodied nature of the telephone voice, devoid of the visual cues of body language, could also evoke feelings of anxiety or mistrust. The telephone thus established a new dialectic of closeness and distance, availability and threatened privacy, which will become one of the central issues of modern life. In its essence, the telephone democratized synchronous long-distance communication, transferring it from an exclusively institutional framework to the hands of ordinary people. Its appearance has not only changed the way people talk, but also what they talk about and with whom. It established the foundations for a culture of constant availability and networking, the ultimate consequences of which we will only experience with the advent of mobile and Internet technologies a century later. Therefore, the telephone can rightly be considered the first true “intimate technology” - a device that reshaped the very foundations of human closeness. Schematic representation of the influence of the telephone

Figure 2.15: Schematic representation of the influence of the telephone on private and public communication, the abolition of the necessity of physical presence for intimate communication and the new dialectic of closeness and threatened privacy.

2.6 Radio and television as catalysts of mass experience

Entering the twentieth century, the concept of space, time and community was reshaped by the appearance of two media that will mark the epoch: radio and television. Their development further initiated a deep transformation of social reality, establishing new forms of collective experience of the world. It was radio and television that became the first true catalysts of mass experience, capable of simultaneously connecting millions of people in the unique act of listening or watching. The advent of radio in the first decades of the century brought a revolution in sound. For the first time in history, a human voice, music or news of a distant event could overcome physical barriers and enter directly into the privacy of the home. Radio broke the silence and filled everyday life with a new soundscape, but its real power lay in its ability to create a shared imaginative space. Listening to the broadcast of an important political speech, sports match or radio drama, an individual became aware that at the same moment thousands, even millions of strangers were sharing this experience with him. This awareness of simultaneity created a bond that did not exist before, an invisible network that connected the dispersed audience into a single listening body. In the middle of the century, television supplemented that sound image with the visual power of the moving image, which made its influence even more immediate and comprehensive. The television soon assumed the role of a central place in the home, becoming a “window to the world” through which scenes of coronations, space flights, wars and cultural spectacles entered the living rooms. The power of television rested in its ability to mediate reality seemingly directly and unfiltered. The visual experience of events like the 1969 moon landing did not leave much room for individual interpretation; he offered a ready-made, common image of reality that was engraved in the collective memory. In this way, television has become the ultimate synchronizing mechanism, uniting national and global communities in a shared, visually authenticated experience. It is precisely this synchronized and collective participation in a media-mediated event that forms the core of the mass experience. It is not exhausted in the fact that a large number of people receive the same information, but in the pervasive awareness of the commonality of that act. This sense of belonging to a temporary but extremely strong community of viewers or listeners strengthened social cohesion and created common reference points in culture. The events broadcast by radio and television became the main topics of conversation, part of the general culture and the basis for building a common identity. Therefore, the role of radio and television went far beyond the passive transmission of content. They acted as active agents of social change. They shaped public opinion, established cultural norms, created heroes and icons, and directed the emotional life of the nation.
