The way these media framed reality, chose topics and presented events had a decisive influence on the perception of the world and one’s own place in it. As media theorists point out, the medium itself, its technological nature and the way it organizes perception becomes a message that reshapes human experience and social relations (McLuhan, 1964). Radio and television did not only report on history; they created it, turning millions of individuals into participants of the same, mass and historical moment.

Figure 2.16: Stages in shaping mass experience through radio and television, from technological innovation to social impact – synchronized and collective participation in a media-mediated event.

2.6.1 The rise of radio and the “voice” of common reality

The appearance of radio as the first truly mass electronic media fundamentally transformed the social reality of the first half of the twentieth century. Its key feature, which distinguished it from all previous forms of communication, was the ability to create simultaneity of experience on a previously unimaginable scale. For the first time in history, millions of people, spatially separated, could listen to the same content at the same moment, thus becoming participants in a unique, shared sound reality. This unique sense of collective participation led Marshall McLuhan (1964) to the famous metaphor of the radio as a “tribal drum”, an instrument that brings together a dispersed community in a unique rhythm and resonance. Radio thereby became a powerful agent of social cohesion, weaving invisible threads that connected individuals in their homes into a large, imagined community of listeners. In times of social crises, wars or major national events, the radio was a focal point that homogenized the national mood and created a sense of destiny connection. At the center of that new media paradigm was the human voice. Freed from the visual context, reduced to its sonic essence, the voice gained exceptional strength and intimacy through radio waves. He was not only a carrier of semantic content, but a powerful medium of emotions, presence and personality. The sound of the voice filling the privacy of the home created the illusion of an immediate, almost personal relationship between the speaker and the millions of individual listeners. This parasocial interaction was key to understanding the impact of radio - the voice became an agent that bridged public and private space, bringing distant events and personalities into the intimate circle of the family hearth. Statesmen and political leaders soon recognized the power of this new medium for shaping public opinion and mobilizing the masses. Voice has become a fundamental political tool. For example, American President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s “Fireside Chats” are a paradigmatic example of using radio to establish trust and leadership. Addressing the nation in a calm and personal tone, Roosevelt managed to create the impression that he was talking to each citizen individually, offering comfort and guidance during the difficult times of the Great Depression. In this context, the voice became a symbol of stability and authority that was both distant and incredibly close at the same time.

Figure 2.17: Schematic representation of the political use of radio: from voice as a medium to influence on public opinion, mobilization and authority.

His influence permeated the entire cultural life, shaping musical taste, popularizing dramatic forms through radio dramas and creating the first stars of the airwaves. Radio thus established a sonic tapestry of common culture, a frame of reference shared by members of different social strata. It is this ability of radio to simultaneously broadcast a unique “voice” - be it the voice of an announcer, politician, actor or singer - and make it part of the private experience of millions, which has created what we can call “the voice of shared reality”. It was a sound reflection and, at the same time, a constitutive element of the consciousness of belonging to a wider social entity.

Figure 2.18: Presentation of the development and influence of the radio medium, from mass listening and intimate voice to the creation of a shared reality and political cohesion.

2.6.2 Television and the visual aspect of shared reality

Television should be understood as a key agent in the shaping of social reality and collective consciousness, which actively constitutes a common symbolic space within which community life takes place. It is precisely in its visual nature that the basis of its power to contribute to the creation of what can be called a shared imagination lies. Unlike print media, which largely shaped national consciousness through language and abstract narratives, television offers a direct, visual insight into the world. This ability to show events, people and spaces, and not just describe them, gives the imagined community a tangible, concrete form. The notion of “imagined community” by Benedict Anderson (1983), originally linked to the rise of the press and capitalism, acquires a new, stronger dimension in the age of television. Millions of people, who will never meet in person, share the same visual repertoire, the same images of the nation, its successes, crises and rituals through the television screen. This creates a deep sense of belonging based on shared viewing and visual experience. Furthermore, the power of television does not derive exclusively from its visuality, but also from its ability to create the illusion of simultaneity. The feeling that an event is happening “live” and that the entire community is watching it at the same moment creates a strong social bond. This sense of sharing the present moment bridges the physical distance between individuals and integrates them into a single, synchronized auditory body. This mechanism is most evident in the phenomenon that Daniel Dayan and Elihu Katz (1992) called “media events”. These are extraordinary occasions - such as state ceremonies, major sports competitions, royal weddings or funerals - that interrupt the usual course of programs and life. These events are shown with great respect and ceremony, turning television viewing into a kind of civil rite. By participating in this ritual, viewers not only receive information, but also confirm the fundamental values and norms of their community, thereby renewing and strengthening social cohesion. Television, therefore, acts as a central mediator in the weaving of the visual and ritual fabric of modern communities. By synthesizing an image that provides evidence and a sense of simultaneity that creates community, it makes the imaginary community visible and present in the daily life of its members.

Figure 2.19: Schematic representation of the role of television in the constitution of the shared imagination, connecting its fundamental mechanisms (visuality and simultaneity) with social outcomes (strengthening of imagined community and cohesion).

2.6.3 Forerunner of the information society

The emergence of the information society, although it is often associated with the second half of the twentieth century and the accelerated development of digital technology, has its deep roots in the theoretical assumptions and visionary ideas that preceded it. These ideas, formed before there were technical possibilities for their full implementation, created the intellectual foundation for understanding information as a central resource and a key driver of social change. Among the thinkers whose work was decisive, Vannevar Bush and Norbert Wiener stand out, whose concepts permanently shaped the architecture of the contemporary digital world. Vannevar Bush in his famous essay As We May Think (Bush, 1945) presents a vision that prophetically announced the future of knowledge management. The central concept of that essay is memex, an imagined device that embodies a completely new way of organizing and retrieving human knowledge. Bush described memex as a privatized, mechanized archive – a kind of desk where an individual could store all their books, records and communications. Its true novelty, however, does not lie in the mere possibility of storage, but in the principle of associative indexing. This mechanism, opposed to rigid alphabetical or numerical classification systems, was supposed to imitate the non-linear and jumpy connections created by the human mind. The user could create traces or paths between different documents, thus linking related ideas and data regardless of their original form or location. It was this idea of interconnected information that directly inspired the later creators of hypertext, such as Ted Nelson and Douglas Engelbart, and today is reflected in the very structure of the World Wide Web. Almost at the same time, Norbert Wiener (1948) in his work Cybernetics: Or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine lays the foundations of cybernetics, a scientific discipline that studies the principles of control and communication in living beings and machines. Wiener’s thought is focused on the universal laws that govern complex systems, regardless of whether they are biological or mechanical in nature. At the center of cybernetic thought is the notion of a feedback loop (feedback loop), a fundamental mechanism of self-regulation that enables the system to adapt and maintain stability based on received information about its own actions. By studying how systems collect, process and use information to guide their behavior, cybernetics has provided a theoretical framework for the development of artificial intelligence, robotics and computer networks. She introduced the notion of a system as an agent that actively operates within its environment, thus laying the foundation stone for understanding machines that can learn and make decisions independently. Although they operated in the period before the full digital revolution, Bush’s vision of networked knowledge and Wiener’s theory of self-managing information systems form the two fundamental pillars on which the architecture of the information society was later built. Bush predicted how we would access information, while Wiener explained how systems, including technological ones, could manage that information. Their work testifies to the fact that the information society is primarily the result of intellectual evolution, and only then of the technological revolution.

Figure 2.20: The intellectual foundations of the information society – Bush’s memex and Wiener’s cybernetics as a foundation for networked knowledge and self-regulating systems.

2.7 Internet and digital revolution

At the very turn of the 20th and 21st centuries, at a time when it seemed that the fundamental communication challenges had already been solved by the establishment of fast and global connections via telephone, radio and television, a completely new communication ecosystem appeared on the horizon: the Internet. In a period of just a few decades, this system, originally conceived as an experimental project of the American agency ARPA (Advanced Research Projects Agency), has grown into a fundamental infrastructure for information exchange, collaboration and social change (Leiner et al., 2009). Its origin, ARPANET, was designed as a research network to connect scientists and universities across the United States. Among the first institutions to join the project were the University of California (UCLA) and the Stanford Research Institute (SRI), which enabled their researchers to exchange data and coordinate experimental work much faster. In 1969, the first, now legendary network message was sent. The attempt to send the word “LOGIN” was interrupted after entering the letter “LO” due to a system crash, but this technical failure was recorded as a symbolic beginning of a new era. What in the early seventies seemed like a technological idea reserved for a narrow circle of the scientific community, soon transformed into a fundamental invention that will mark the entire subsequent period of digital communication.

Figure 2.21: Schematic representation of the development of the ARPANET: from the ARPA research network and university connectivity to the first network message in 1969 and the foundations of digital communication.

A turning point in its development took place in 1989, when Tim Berners-Lee, a scientist employed at CERN, designed the World Wide Web (Berners-Lee, 1990) and thus transformed it into a platform accessible to every user. Using hypertext links and simple Internet browsers, people were given the opportunity for the first time to navigate distant digital spaces, simultaneously sharing documents, images, and even early forms of multimedia content. The power of the Internet is not only manifested in its technical basis, but primarily in its ability to fundamentally reshape social, economic and cultural paradigms. By enabling an almost instantaneous and unhindered exchange of information on a global scale, the Internet has abolished previous spatial and temporal limitations, establishing a new information society in which access to knowledge and data becomes a key resource (Castells, 2010). This has dramatically changed the ways in which individuals and communities communicate, work and spend their free time, creating entirely new forms of social interaction and cultural expression. The development of online platforms and tools in the last three decades has proven to be the central driver of profound transformations in the way people communicate with each other, collaborate and jointly shape social relationships. Although these processes have opened up enormous opportunities for networking, exchange of ideas and the creation of global communities, at the same time they have fueled numerous controversies, primarily those related to issues of privacy and the quality of newly formed relationships. In economic terms, the digital revolution fueled by the Internet has led to the creation of new markets and business models that were unimaginable in the analog age. E-commerce, the sharing economy and remote working are just a few examples of disruptive innovations that have transformed entire industries. In such an environment, the role and skills of business agents also had to adapt. Successful operation in the modern market today implies a high level of digital literacy - the ability to navigate the digital ecosystem, use specialized tools and understand new forms of market communication. Although the reach of the digital revolution is undoubtedly enormous, it would be wrong to ignore its darker sides and the challenges it poses to modern society. One of the fundamental problems is the so-called digital divide, i.e. the growing difference between those who have access to information technology and the benefits it provides and those who are excluded from this process due to economic, social or geographical reasons (Norris, 2001). Furthermore, ubiquitous digitization has also opened up complex issues of privacy protection, as vast sets of personal data are constantly being collected and processed. In parallel, the ease of information dissemination via the Internet has created fertile ground for misinformation and malicious propaganda, which threatens the foundations of public debate and trust in institutions. The fight against fake news and cyber threats requires not only the development of new technological and regulatory frameworks but also the systematic strengthening of the media and digital literacy of the entire population. The ability to critically evaluate information therefore becomes a key skill for navigating the complexity of the digital age.

2.7.1 Expansion of communication channels

E-mail stands out among the first mass-accepted Internet services, which in the nineties of the 20th century introduced a radical shift in everyday business and personal information exchange. Unlike traditional mail and fax, e-mail has enabled instant delivery of messages regardless of geographic distance (Shapiro & Varian, 1999). For example, global companies have begun to connect their offices on different continents almost in real time, speeding up decision-making and raising the level of coordination between teams. At the same time, private users used e-mail to communicate with family and friends on a daily basis, making the world a smaller place at minimal cost and with unparalleled speed of data exchange.

Modern business completely changes the way companies communicate with clients: communication is moving away from a one-time sales transaction towards a complex process of building long-term relationships. Therefore, presence and availability on multiple communication platforms are no longer a competitive advantage, but a necessity. This approach is called multi-channel communication in professional literature and is considered one of the key factors for high client satisfaction. It includes traditional channels such as telephone and e-mail, but also extends to more dynamic platforms such as social networks, online chat services and mobile applications intended for users.

Multichannel communication: Strategy of the simultaneous presence of an organization or agent on multiple communication platforms (telephone, e-mail, social networks, chat, mobile applications) in order to enable users to freely choose the channel that suits them best; a higher degree of integration, known as an omnichannel approach, aims for a unique and seamless user experience where the boundaries between channels are almost imperceptible.

Introducing a multi-channel approach brings significant business breakthroughs. It expands the reach and visibility of the company towards a wider circle of potential users and significantly enriches the overall user experience. Namely, clients are given the freedom to choose the communication path that suits them best at a given moment, which contributes to the feeling of comfort and adaptability of the service to their needs. However, it should be emphasized that the implementation of a multi-channel strategy is a significant organizational issue. It requires the systematic education of agents who must be trained in the skillful use of all available tools. In doing so, it is crucial to ensure that messages and information provided to clients are aligned and consistent across all channels. Consistency in information and service quality, regardless of the chosen channel, becomes the basis of trust. Any deviation, i.e. providing contradictory or inconsistent answers, inevitably creates a feeling of insecurity and frustration in the client, which in the long run can damage the company’s reputation. Therefore, real and meaningful integration across multiple channels is actually set as the ultimate goal. This higher level of development, known as the omnichannel approach, implies the creation of a unique and flawless user experience in which the boundaries between individual channels are almost imperceptible. In a fully integrated system, the agent communicating with the customer has a complete view of all previous interactions, regardless of whether they took place via live chat, email or phone call. A client can start an inquiry on one platform, continue it on another and conclude on a third without having to repeat information, making the entire process fluid and user-centric.

Figure 2.22: Schematic representation of the transition from multi-channel communication to an omni-channel approach, with channel integration, complete insight and seamless transitions for the user.

2.7.2 Collaboration and collaborative tools

In the upgrade to e-mail, various collaborative systems such as chat-rooms (Chat-room), forums and instant messages (e.g. ICQ, AIM, MSN Messenger) appeared. These early forms of digital exchange soon contributed to the development of innovative platforms for group work in the cloud, such as Basecamp or Slack, which significantly simplified team collaboration on projects, especially when it comes to software development, organization of international conferences or coordination of distance learning (Benkler, 2006). The term cooperation in the context of multi-agent systems means the basic principle of action in which two or more agents, be they artificial or human, coordinate their activities in order to achieve a common goal. Cooperation is fundamentally different from coordination because it does not only mean avoiding conflict in action, but also active and purposeful exchange of information and resources. The basic premise of any cooperation is the existence of a common goal to which all involved agents strive. Achieving such a goal, which goes beyond the possibilities of individual action, necessarily implies a dynamic exchange of knowledge and information. This exchange enables agents to make better decisions.

Cooperation in multi-agent systems: The principle of joint action of two or more agents (human or artificial) that coordinate activities to achieve a goal that exceeds the possibilities of individual action; it differs from mere coordination because it involves the active exchange of information and resources, negotiation and conflict resolution mechanisms, and the building of trust among participants (Benkler, 2006; Wooldridge, 2009).

However, the collaborative process is not without its challenges, among which the possibility of conflicting interests or agendas among the agents stands out. Therefore, the existence of pre-defined or dynamically established mechanisms for negotiation and conflict resolution is necessary for successful cooperation. These mechanisms ensure that partial interests are subordinated to the general goal and that the coherence of joint action is maintained.

Figure 2.23: Basic elements that make up the process of cooperation in multiagent systems: common goal, information exchange, negotiation and conflict resolution mechanisms, and collaborative tools.

In practical application, especially in complex environments where both humans and artificial agents operate, these principles are realized by using collaborative tools. These are software solutions and platforms designed to facilitate and structure interaction between participants. Their function is manifested on several levels: from tools for simultaneous editing and sharing of documents, through systems for delegating and monitoring tasks, all the way to communication platforms that enable asynchronous and synchronous communication. The role of these tools is to encourage and maintain trust, which is crucial for any long-term and fruitful cooperation.

Collaborative tools: Software solutions and platforms designed for the structured joint action of multiple participants - from tools for simultaneous editing of documents and file sharing, through systems for delegation and monitoring of tasks, to communication platforms for synchronous and asynchronous exchange; in the context of multi-agent systems, collaborative tools encourage and maintain trust and enable effective coordination between human and artificial agents (Benkler, 2006).

2.7.3 Mass communication and homogenization of culture

Mass communication, as one of the fundamental processes that shape modern societies, represents a complex phenomenon whose influence extends to all aspects of social life, and especially to the field of culture. By means of technological innovations - from print and radio to television and the Internet - channels were created that enabled almost simultaneous transmission of messages to a vast, spatially dispersed and heterogeneous crowd. In this process, the mass media are not only channels for the transmission of information, but act as powerful agents of social change, actively participating in the creation, shaping and dissemination of cultural patterns, values and worldviews. The central consequence of such action, which is hotly debated in sociological and cultural thought, is the homogenization of culture. It is a process of gradual reduction of cultural diversity and suppression of autochthonous, local cultural expressions under the influence of dominant, globally expanded cultural contents. Mass communication, in its essence, becomes the main bearer and mediator of these dominant contents, thereby creating a global shared symbolic environment. Unique cultural patterns, which originate predominantly from Western, especially Anglo-American cultural centers, spread on a planetary level and are adopted in different parts of the world. This process is most clearly manifested in several key domains. In the field of audiovisual culture, the Hollywood film industry and the global music scene impose aesthetic standards, narrative structures and musical genres that become universally recognizable and accepted. Similarly, in the sphere of consumer culture, global brands and marketing campaigns promote unique lifestyles, fashion trends, and consumer habits, erasing regional and national particularities in dress, diet, and everyday practices (Thompson, 1995). The influence on language, as the fundamental bearer of cultural identity, is particularly significant. The spread of English as a global lingua franca through media content leads to the mass adoption of English in national languages. This seemingly unequivocal linguistic borrowing becomes a process that can affect the deeper semantic and syntactic structures of the language, changing the ways in which thoughts and feelings are expressed within a particular language community. This exposes linguistic diversity, one of humanity’s greatest assets, to the pressure of unification.

However, it would be wrong to consider the process of cultural homogenization as one-way and absolute. Contemporary theories of globalization warn of the existence of resistance and counter-tendencies, whereby local cultures often actively reinterpret global influences, adapt them to their own contexts, and combine them with indigenous elements. This complex process is called hybridization or glocalization - a phenomenon in which the global and the local intertwine, creating new, unique cultural forms (Robertson, 1994). For example, globally popular music genres are enriched with traditional instruments or local chants, and international television formats are adapted to national humor and social specifics.

Figure 2.24: Presentation of the relationship between mass communication, homogenization and glocalization of culture - media and ideational landscapes and the hybridization of the global and the local.

The relationship between mass communication and culture remains inherently dialectical. While the mass media undoubtedly possess enormous potential for unifying cultural practices and values on a global scale, they also provide platforms for the affirmation and visibility of local identities. Cultural homogenization therefore remains a permanent tension between the forces of global integration and the need to preserve local distinctiveness, a tension that will decisively shape the cultural landscape of the 21st century.

Figure 2.25: Presentation of the relationship between mass communication, homogenization and glocalization of culture - the dialectic of global integration and local particularity.

2.7.4 Political sphere and electronic public opinion

The emergence and pervasiveness of the Internet fundamentally transformed the landscape of political communication, introducing new paradigms in shaping, expressing and measuring public opinion. The digital age has put an end to the former exclusive dependence of political actors on traditional mass media as intermediaries in the transmission of messages to voters. Instead of a one-way channel, political communication now takes place within a complex, multi-directional and interactive network structure. In this new environment, a phenomenon that we call electronic public opinion - a dynamic and often elusive sum of attitudes, feelings and opinions expressed on digital platforms such as social networks, forums, blogs and portals with comments - arises and operates. The key determinant of this transformation is the change in the role of the citizens themselves. From the position of mostly passive recipients of political messages, they become active agents in the political process. The ability to instantly comment, share content, create their own narratives and organize collective actions gives them power that they did not have in the pre-internet era. This displaces the political discussion from formalized frameworks, such as parliament or media debates, into a much wider, more open, but also more chaotic space of the Internet. In such a space, official political narratives confront unfiltered experiences, criticisms and alternative viewpoints of citizens, which creates a polyphonic, but also polarized public sphere. As Castells (2009) notes, power in the information age is increasingly found in communication networks, and the ability to influence public discourse becomes a key resource of political struggle.

Figure 2.26: Schematic representation of the transformation of citizens from passive recipients to active political agents through commenting, sharing content, collective actions and acting in networks.

Figure 2.27: Transformation of the communication model in the political sphere – from a one-way channel to a multi-directional, interactive network structure and electronic public opinion.

Furthermore, electronic public opinion has properties that significantly differentiate it from that measured by traditional survey research. Its main feature is the speed of creation and changeability; it reacts to events in real time and can change drastically within hours under the influence of new information or viral content. It is also more transparent in its creation because it is based on publicly available data - posts, comments, likes and shares. However, these very properties make it susceptible to manipulation. Organized groups, be it political parties, interest lobbies or foreign actors, can use automated accounts (bots) or coordinated campaigns to create a false impression of mass support or resistance to an idea, law or candidate. The structure of the Internet public sphere also brings other challenges. In contrast to Habermas’ ideal image of a unified public sphere in which rational discussion leads to consensus, the digital space is extremely fragmented. Users tend to gather in like-minded communities, creating so-called echo chambers or filter bubbles, where they are exposed only to those information and attitudes that confirm their existing beliefs (Sunstein, 2017). Such informational isolation makes it difficult for different social groups to understand each other and strongly contributes to political polarization. The speed and reach of digital communication, although carrying enormous potential for democratization, at the same time open up space for the unprecedented spread of misinformation and fake news, the verification of which for the average user represents a significant cognitive effort. The political sphere consequently faces a double challenge: on the one hand, it must adapt to new forms of citizen participation and use their democratic potential, while on the other hand, it must develop mechanisms to defend against manipulations and preserve the quality of public debate in the digital environment.

Figure 2.28: Schematic representation of the fragmentation of the Internet public sphere: from echo chambers and filter bubbles to polarization and difficult mutual understanding.

2.7.5 Global spread and cultural influence

The universal networking of the modern world, achieved through digital technologies and the Internet, is a fundamental prerequisite for the global dissemination of cultural content and ideas. This digital infrastructure breaks down spatial and temporal barriers, enabling the almost instantaneous dissemination of information at an unprecedented level. This creates frameworks within which cultural phenomena, regardless of their origin, acquire the potential for planetary distribution. Various agents operate within this newly established communication framework, such as social media platforms, influential individuals (influencers) and specialized internet communities. Their role on the superficial level is manifested in mediating or distributing content, but they are essentially active participants in the processes of creating, adapting and reshaping the meaning of cultural products. Through their action, the contents are spread, but also interpreted, commented on and incorporated into new semantic networks. As already mentioned, globally available cultural phenomena go through the process of localization, i.e. adaptation to specific cultural, linguistic and social contexts. This combination of the global and the local is called glocalization, and it manifests itself, for example, in the way internet memes are translated and adapted to resonate with local humor and social circumstances (Shifman, 2014). The content thus retains its recognizable core, but at the same time takes on new, locally determined meanings. Such permeation is the origin of hybrid cultural forms that combine elements of different traditions. This eliminates the sharp dichotomy between, for example, Western and non-Western culture, because cultural influence becomes multidirectional and mutual. The global scene is increasingly becoming an arena where different cultural expressions meet, mix and create new, syncretic forms that testify to the complexity of contemporary identities. The described processes also challenge simplistic views such as technological determinism - the point of view according to which technology unequivocally shapes society and culture. On the contrary, it is evident that users and communities actively appropriate technology, adapt it to their needs and use it in unforeseen ways, thereby becoming agents of cultural and social change themselves (Baym, 2015). The complexity of these relationships can be shown in the following diagram:

Figure 2.29: The process of cultural dissemination and hybridization, from the original cultural product through the agents of dissemination and the process of adaptation to the localized version and the hybrid cultural form.

Finally, the global distribution of cultural content also opens up complex ethical issues. Concepts such as cultural appropriation, decontextualization and commodification of traditional practices are becoming central topics in discussions about the consequences of digital cultural permeation, seeking a constant reconsideration of power relations in the globalized world.

2.7.6 Expansion of social networks

After the consolidation of the fast digital communication paradigm, the late 1990s and early 2000s saw the emergence of the early generation of social networks, such as SixDegrees.com (launched in 1997). Named after the concept of six degrees of separation, suggesting that any two people on Earth can be connected by a chain of six or fewer acquaintances, the site allowed users to create profiles, connect to lists of friends and family, effectively laying the groundwork for the concept of online social networking. Although initially limited in reach, SixDegrees paved the way for later mega-platforms such as MySpace (2003) and Facebook (2004), on which the momentum of mass online socializing was traced (Boyd & Ellison, 2007). The real turning point was the appearance of Facebook in 2004, a platform that fundamentally changed the paradigm of digital interaction. The success of that network rested on a previously new approach: instead of creating anonymous virtual identities, the focus was placed on mapping and establishing existing social connections within the digital environment. This encouraged the use of real names and connecting with people from the user’s immediate social reality, which created a sense of authenticity and trust that previous networks lacked (Boyd & Ellison, 2007).

Further diversification of forms of digital communication was manifested in the emergence of Twitter, which introduced a concise microblogging format. By limiting messages to a small number of characters, it enabled an unprecedented speed of flow of information, news and personal announcements in real time. At the same time, technological progress, primarily the widespread availability of smartphones, has directed development towards mobile applications and visual content. Platforms like Instagram and Snapchat built their foundations precisely on the exchange of photos and short videos. They thus went beyond the mere function of a communication tool and became prominent spaces for the construction and expression of personal and collective identity (Van Dijck, 2013). Development also went in the direction of functional specialization, which is most evident in the establishment of professional networks such as LinkedIn, which have become an indispensable arena for career development, business networking and presentation of professional achievements. The contemporary moment is marked by the predominance of platforms based on short video format, among which TikTok stands out. Its peculiarity lies not only in its content, but primarily in the way it is distributed, where the algorithmic system takes a central role. In such a model, the algorithm becomes the key agent that mediates between the content and the user, actively and constantly shaping his entire experience with personalized recommendations. Finally, it is important to point out that the implications of the expansion of social networks are social, cultural and political. These platforms have assumed the role of central arenas for public discourse, political organizing and social activism, and at the same time have become fertile ground for the systematic spread of misinformation and manipulative content (Zuboff, 2019). Therefore, their influence on contemporary society should be understood in all its complexity and contradictions, as a phenomenon that reshapes the ways in which we communicate, work, create communities and understand ourselves.

Figure 2.30: Schematic representation of the development of social networks from SixDegrees and Facebook towards visual platforms, short video, algorithmic distribution and effects on public discourse and misinformation.

2.7.7 Digital Tribes and Knowledge Squares: Anatomy of Successful Online Communities

Soon after the initial formation of broad and general digital markets, the Internet landscape began to blossom into specialized ecosystems—virtual communities dedicated to creating, sharing, evaluating, and discussing very specific types of content or interests. Platforms have become fascinating social laboratories where users gather, developing their own governance mechanisms, reputation systems, and unique microcultures that shape behavior and interaction within their digital walls. Take Reddit for example. That platform is not so much a single community as a vast, sprawling digital metropolis composed of thousands, if not millions, of thematic sub-communities known as subreddits. Each subreddit functions as a separate neighborhood or even a miniature digital city-state, often with its own carefully crafted set of rules, norms of behavior, and a team of volunteer moderators who act as a kind of local government (Massanari, 2017). The spectrum is incredible: from strictly moderated academic forums like r/science or r/AskHistorians, where detailed references and in-depth analysis are required, to chaotic and humorous corners like r/funny or niche communities dedicated to the narrowest possible interests. What gives Reddit its dynamism is its basic upvote/downvote mechanism, which acts as a collective curation machine: content that the community finds valuable or interesting rises to the top, while less relevant or low-quality content is relegated to the digital background. It is a continuous referendum on relevance. If we compare Reddit to a bustling city with countless different neighborhoods, then Stack Overflow (part of the wider Stack Exchange network) is its precisely organized technical library, or perhaps a highly specialized guild home for developers. Born from the need for quick and accurate answers to specific technical questions, Stack Overflow has become an almost unavoidable reference point in the world of software development (Mamykina et al., 2011). Its success lies in its rigorous focus on quality and meritocracy. The system of scoring (reputation) and accepting the best answers creates a strong incentive to provide accurate, clear and useful solutions. The community actively maintains a high signal-to-noise ratio, discouraging vague questions or opinion-based answers, creating an extremely efficient mechanism for collective problem-solving and archiving of specific technical knowledge. Discord followed a different evolutionary path. Originally launched as a tool for voice communication among video game players, it quickly outgrew its initial niche and became a platform for a wide range of communities (Seering et al., 2019). Unlike asynchronous forums like Reddit or Stack Overflow, Discord offers a sense of real-time presence and interaction, more akin to a network of vibrant digital clubs or community hubs. Its server-based structure, with channels organized by topic (text, voice, video) and the ability to integrate bots for task automation and moderation, has proven to be extremely flexible. Today, it is used not only by players, but also by educational institutions, art collectives, support groups, and even companies for internal communication and external community building, creating spaces for more fluid and immediate interaction. Finally, we must not forget open-source projects and collaborative repositories like GitHub. Although they are not social networks in the classical sense, platforms like GitHub function as huge digital construction sites and workshops, and at the same time as powerful communication networks that connect millions of developers and technical experts around the world (Dabbish et al., 2012). The combination of code versioning tools (such as Git), issue trackers, pull requests, and integrated discussion forums creates a highly structured communication framework optimized for complex technical collaboration. The success of projects like the operating system Linux, the web-framework React or the AI library TensorFlow testifies to the incredible power of this model of distributed collective intelligence, where thousands of individuals, often without direct contact, manage to build together some of the most complex software artifacts today. GitHub in this new ecosystem of machine-machine collaboration turns into a kind of operational base of autonomous code agents: Google’s Jules, for example, opens pull-requests and automatically suggests corrections based on the analysis of the complete repository, relying on GitHub’s API for versioning and code review flows. A similar symbiosis is already demonstrated by OpenAI-ev Codex – the engine that powers Copilot – because it learns from public repositories and generates ready-made code in a format that can be immediately incorporated into those same projects. New tools called vibe-coding (vibe-coding) like Windsurf or Cursor go a step further: the agent analyzes the history of commits, writes tests and runs CI pipelines, making GitHub a shared working memory through which people and models are coordinated in real time. Such an infrastructure allows software development to gradually move from manual code editing to process orchestration, where people set goals and a distributed agent swarm on GitHub realizes tasks – from bug discovery to documentation writing – with transparent audit history and collective approval mechanisms. These diverse examples – from the city-states of Reddit and the guilds of Stack Overflow, through the clubs of Discord to the global construction sites of GitHub – illustrate the richness and inventiveness of digital forms of association in online communities. In these virtual spaces, individuals, driven by common interests, passions or goals, establish lasting connections, build social capital and participate in the collective creation of value (Rheingold, 2000). In order to penetrate into the anatomy of their success, it is necessary to look at the fundamental elements that make them stable and purposeful. A fundamental prerequisite for the creation and survival of any living online community is the existence of a strong and clearly defined common interest. Whether it’s professional collaboration, hobbyist passion or mutual support, it’s this central gathering point that gives the community its identity and meaning. It acts as a gravitational center that attracts new members and retains existing ones, ensuring internal cohesion. Without this common purpose, the community dissipates into a multitude of unrelated interactions and loses its reason for existence. The key pillar of every successful community is built on this foundation: mutual trust and social capital. Trust is not a given, it is gradually acquired through repeated positive interactions, reliability and respect for established norms. The accumulation of such experiences creates social capital, that is, a network of relationships and reciprocity that enables members to cooperate effectively and feel safe (Putnam, 2000). In such an environment, members are more willing to share valuable information, openly ask for help, and invest their own time and effort for the benefit of the whole. Each digital tribe develops its own system of rules and norms of behavior, whether they are explicitly codified in the form of forum rules or exist as tacit, implicit agreements. These rules regulate communication, resolve conflicts and protect the community from destructive behavior. In addition to formal rules, the development of specific language, jargon and symbols that are understandable only to members is of crucial importance. Such an internal code not only facilitates and accelerates communication on complex topics, but also strongly strengthens the sense of belonging and collective identity, clearly demarcating “us” from “them”.

The role of agents, both human and software, in maintaining community health is extremely important. Human agents, such as moderators or community managers, act as gardeners of the digital space: they encourage discussion, guide new members, calm tensions and remove unwanted content. Their presence and active engagement guarantee that the community remains a safe and productive space. On the other hand, software agents, through algorithms for filtering, recommending content or connecting users with similar interests, automate key functions and allow the community to scale to a large number of members. Finally, the success of a community is reflected in the value it creates for its members and, sometimes, for the general public. This value can take different forms: from solving specific problems and sharing professional knowledge to providing emotional support and a sense of belonging. In their most developed forms, online communities become the scene of the emergence of collective intelligence, where the synergy of individual contributions leads to insights and solutions that exceed the capabilities of any individual (Lévy, 1997). Seen in this way, online communities stop being just a technological phenomenon and become key factors in the knowledge society, capable of solving complex challenges through collaboration and trust built in the digital world.

Figure 2.31: Schematic representation of the emergence of the collective value of an online community: from shared purpose and interaction to trust, social capital and shared benefit.

2.7.8 Porous membranes: when digital becomes real (and vice versa)

Once upon a time, the Internet was thought of as a separate space, a cybernetic world that one entered and exited from. But as digital platforms became more deeply woven into the fabric of our everyday lives, that boundary began to melt, becoming increasingly porous, like a membrane through which ideas, relationships, and identities constantly penetrate in both directions. Virtual communities were no longer just remote sanctuaries; their inhabitants began to spill over into the physical world, organizing meetups, conferences, protests, and get-togethers that blurred the distinction between online acquaintances and offline friends (Rainie & Wellman, 2012). The arrival of smartphones, those ubiquitous portals in our pockets that ensure our constant connection, has only ended the last illusions about a clear dividing line. Our online and offline lives are no longer parallel worlds; they are inextricably intertwined. Platforms like Meetup.com have become a perfect example of this phenomenon. They function as digital catalysts for physical interaction, bringing together people with similar interests – whether they’re rare dog lovers, programmers learning a new language, activists organizing a cleanup, or book club members. The initial contact and group formation happens online, but the real goal is to meet face-to-face: gathering in coffee shops, parks, libraries or workshops (Quan-Haase & Wellman, 2002). There, abstract avatars and text conversations turn into real handshakes, shared laughs and lively discussions, demonstrating how the digital can enrich, not just replace, physical sociality and community building. It is a picture of networked individualism where connections are formed around common interests, regardless of geographic proximity, but often materialize in physical space (Wellman, 2001). However, this blurring of boundaries has not gone without causing deep discomfort and serious questions. While some celebrated new forms of connection, others expressed concerns about the authenticity of relationships nurtured through screens and the potential for the erosion of privacy in a world of constant digital surveillance. Is the person we know through a carefully curated online profile the same person we meet in person? In her influential works, Sherry Turkle warned of the phenomenon of alone together, where technology creates the illusion of connection while actually isolating us, encouraging us to prefer orderly, controlled online interactions over the messy unpredictability of real human relationships (Turkle, 2011). Privacy concerns have exploded into the public consciousness with scandals such as Cambridge Analytica, which exposed how personal data collected from Facebook (often without user consent or understanding) can be used for sophisticated psychological profiling and targeted political persuasion, potentially influencing the outcome of elections (Cadwalladr & Graham-Harrison, 2018). This and similar incidents have illuminated the background of the business models of many platforms, based on what Shoshana Zuboff calls surveillance capitalism: the extraction and monetization of human experience transformed into data, often through unclear terms of use and interfaces designed to encourage us to share more than we would consciously consent to (Zuboff, 2019). Our online activity, our likes, clicks, and even keeping our eyes on certain content, become raw material for algorithms that profile us and predict our behavior, shaping the information we see and the products we are offered. At the same time, the constant presence of the digital world has fueled discussions about digital alienation, addiction and the impact on mental health. The design of many social networks, with endless scrolling, notifications, and variable reward mechanisms (like likes), can create compulsive behavior loops (Alter, 2017). The pressure to maintain a perfect virtual identity, constant comparison with others and fear of missing out (FOMO - Fear Of Missing Out) are associated with increased anxiety and depression, especially among younger users (Twenge, 2019). The line between using technology as a tool and becoming its prisoner is becoming dangerously thin. Thus, while the Internet has undoubtedly broken down barriers and enabled new forms of community and collaboration, it has simultaneously created a complex and often ambivalent space in which our digital and physical lives are constantly interwoven. The dividing line between the digital and the real world, once thought of as a solid and insurmountable border, today is increasingly manifested as a porous membrane. Through it, a constant and two-way permeation takes place, which changes the ontological status of both worlds. It is no longer about the interaction of two separate entities, but about the creation of a hybrid space in which digital bits materialize and physical reality is translated into information code. This process of mutual overflow questions fundamental assumptions about the nature of reality, presence and action.

Figure 2.32: Schematic representation of the transition from a solid boundary between the digital and the real world to a porous membrane, two-way permeation and hybrid space.

2.7.9 Digital revolution and global communication network

The entry into the digital age has brought an atmosphere of continuous connectivity and accelerated global interactions, whereby the Internet and digital tools have become the logistical and cultural fabric of modern society. The shift from physical infrastructure and traditional forms of business to virtual ecosystems has created an environment where collaboration takes place independent of time and space, and the range of information is available on a scale that would have seemed unimaginable just a few decades ago. Such pervasiveness of communication and information flows continues civilization’s long line of innovation, but now it seems that the pace of change has intensified to the extent that it is fundamentally transforming many aspects of human experience. In the context of business and work processes, the construction of virtual market platforms illustrates these deeper changes. Examples of companies like Amazon and eBay show how the global distribution of goods and services has entered a new phase, characterized by hybrid models that connect traditional and digital trade modalities. At the same time, the practice of collaboration through online applications for conversations, document sharing and video conferencing has spread. By selecting collaborators regardless of their geographical location, organizations are increasingly fostering “dispersed teams”, in which knowledge merges into a single whole. These practices parallel the accelerated “cultural globalization”, in which local work culture meets universal standards of digital collaboration, bringing new challenges to organizations that strive to harmonize various work traditions with the fluidity of virtual collaboration.

Education has undergone a similar turn. Online courses and open educational resources provide access to content previously available mostly at elite institutions. The great popularity of platforms like Courser, edX and Khan Academy shows that the demand for flexible, adaptable and above all affordable forms of learning is constantly increasing. Many students and professionals for whom formal, long-term studies are not an option are now choosing microcolleges and specialized courses to adapt more quickly to the changing demands of the labor market or to follow their own interests in the arts, sciences or humanities. Changes in the media sphere are equally diverse. Increasing digital competition has put traditional newspapers, television companies and radio stations in front of the task of radical adaptation to new communication customs and advertising models. With the appearance of internet channels, blogs, podcasts and platforms for videostreaming, space has opened up for countless forms of creative expression. Discussions now take place on Internet forums (Rheingold, 1993), where professional knowledge or niche passions are exchanged, and news broadcasts are often replaced by interactive broadcasts in real time, whereby the audience experienced a transformation from a passive observer to an active participant.

New economic circumstances were by no means absent. The concept of the sharing economy and platforms like Uber and Airbnb (Sundararajan, 2016) have shaken some established rules about ownership, rental and work, showing how agile digital mediation is in connecting supply and demand, even if it raises issues of regulation and protection of workers’ rights. At the same time, open collaboration movements have reached a peak in open-source projects, where global communities develop complex software solutions without traditional hierarchical structures (Benkler, 2006). Such practice has shown that knowledge and innovation can flourish when monopolistic controls are broken and resources are freely available.

Similar collective mechanisms appear in the sphere of financing. Crowdfunding campaigns through platforms like Kickstarter and Indiegogo (Howe, 2008) reveal how a wider audience, not exclusively banks or corporate investors, takes on the role of micro-investors in creative and entrepreneurial projects. Such initiatives revitalize a culture of personal engagement, where supporters donate funds and spread the word about new ideas and actively build a community around them. In one dimension, this brings the empowerment of small innovators, and in another, it imposes the need to restore trust and transparency: in a digital world full of information, it is easy and uncertain to assess who offers what value and with what motives. All these phenomena point to the fact that the digital era, continuing the centuries-old traditions of communication evolution, is becoming a multi-layered experience – intimate and global, innovative and disruptive, promising and risky. It enables intense collaboration and great feats of knowledge discovery, but requires thoughtful strategies for managing privacy, ethics, and intellectual property. It opens up new frontiers for business, education and media, but invites in-depth discussions about the balance of power in the digital space and the control of infrastructure and resources. At the root of all these developments remains the key understanding that communication, for centuries now, is the guiding thread of the development of civilization, and digital technologies are only the last act in the continuous performance of human creativity and interaction.

2.7.10 Digital duality: the promise of democratization and the shadow of new inequalities

The entry into the digital age is marked by a fundamental tension, a duality that permeates almost every aspect of modern life. Digital technology is the scene of conflicting aspirations that simultaneously offer the promise of liberation and cast the shadow of new forms of subjugation. Digital duality manifests itself as a permanent conflict between the vision of a democratized world, in which knowledge and power are available to everyone, and the actual appearance of new, often invisible, inequalities that deepen existing ones and create new social cleavages. Understanding this duality is crucial for any serious judgment of our time. On the one hand, the digital revolution has enormous democratization potential. By breaking down spatial and temporal barriers, the Internet and its related technologies have created unprecedented opportunities for access to information and knowledge. Global libraries, scientific databases and educational platforms have become available to individuals regardless of their geographical location or material status, promoting the idea of a global republic of knowledge. In the political arena, digital media have enabled new forms of civic participation and activism. The ability to quickly organize, share information outside the control of traditional media and directly address power holders gave a voice to those who rarely had one. The potential is manifested in the ability of social movements to quickly mobilize and articulate their demands, creating a new form of what Manuel Castells (2012) calls “network power”. In economic terms, digital platforms have lowered the entry barriers for entrepreneurship, allowing small producers and creators access to a global market that was once reserved exclusively for large corporations. Digital duality contrasts the positive outcomes of the promise of democratization with the negative consequences of new inequalities

Figure 2.33: Digital duality – the promise of democratization (increased access to information, new platforms for participation, global connectivity) and the shadow of new inequalities (digital divide, algorithmic bias and discrimination, concentration of power and surveillance).

On the other side of this bright picture, however, a dark shadow looms. The promise of full democratization remains largely unfulfilled, while at the same time new, more subtle mechanisms of surveillance and inequality are being established. The first and most obvious is the digital divide, which no longer refers only to mere access to the Internet, but also to differences in digital literacy, skills and the ability to critically evaluate information. Those without the necessary skills or resources remain excluded from the digital society, further deepening their existing marginalization. Furthermore, the architecture of the digital world is increasingly shaped by algorithms that, rather than being impartial arbiters, often reflect and reinforce human biases. Algorithmic systems that decide on employment, credit approval or even the probability of committing a criminal offense can systematically discriminate against certain social groups, creating what Cathy O’Neil (2016) calls “weapons of math destruction”. These automated systems act as invisible bureaucracies, whose decisions are difficult to challenge because they are shrouded in a veil of technical objectivity and business secrecy. Perhaps the most profound threat is the rise of what Shoshana Zuboff (2019) calls surveillance capitalism. In this economic model, human experience becomes a raw material that is freely appropriated, turned into behavioral data, and sold in markets that trade predictions about our future. The power is thereby extremely unevenly distributed: on the one hand, there are technological giants who possess the knowledge and infrastructure for collecting and processing data, and on the other hand, users, individual agents who are often not even aware of the extent of surveillance to which they are exposed. This asymmetry of power undermines the very idea of autonomy and free decision-making, creating a market in which we are not the product, but the possibility of influencing our future behavior. Digital duality is therefore a real tension that shapes our social, political and economic reality, revealing the digital sphere not as a utopian or dystopian destination but as a battlefield. The outcome of this struggle depends on the actions of various agents: on the regulatory decisions of states, on the efforts of civil society in the protection of digital rights, on the ethical responsibility of technological creators and, finally, on raising awareness and critical engagement of the users themselves. Acknowledging this duality means rejecting technological determinism and accepting responsibility for actively shaping the digital future—a future in which the promise of democratization will overcome the shadow of new inequalities.

Figure 2.34: Schematic representation of the digital duality: the tension between the democratizing potential of digital technology and the new forms of inequality that together shape society.

2.7.11 Shadows in a digital Eden: privacy, manipulation and the price of connectivity

The semblance of a digital Eden, a world of unlimited possibilities and universal connectivity, brings with it its shadows, spaces where basic human rights and cognitive autonomy are exposed to unprecedented pressures. At the root of this duality lies the paradigm of surveillance capitalism, an economic order that appropriates human experience as a free raw material for production and sales processes (Zuboff, 2019). The first and most obvious victim of such a system is privacy. Massive and ubiquitous data collection – from location and search patterns to biometric information and emotional reactions – has become a fundamental mechanism for the functioning of the digital space. Users, often without full awareness of the scale and depth of this process, willingly give up fragments of their lives in exchange for seemingly free services, thus becoming raw material in a value chain whose ultimate purpose is to monetize their future behavior. Collected data traces are of course used to optimize services or place customized ads, but their purpose inevitably extends deep into the sphere of behavioral modification and targeted manipulation. Algorithmic systems, acting as invisible agents, construct personalized realities based on detailed psychographic profiles, worlds tailored to evoke certain emotional responses and stimulate desired actions. The scale and consequences of such actions became evident in the case of the company Cambridge Analytica, which tried to influence the outcome of democratic elections by misusing data collected from the social network Facebook (Cadwalladr & Graham-Harrison, 2018). This event exposed the systemic vulnerability of modern societies, showing how data infrastructure can be repurposed as a weapon for psychological and political shaping of the public.

Figure 2.35: Systematic collection and analysis of user data leads to algorithmic profiling resulting in personalized content delivery and behavioral manipulation (surveillance capitalism cycle).

The operation of these algorithms, whose fundamental task is the maximization of user engagement, leads to further structural disturbances in the flow of information. By creating so-called “filter bubbles” (filter bubbles) and “echo chambers” (echo chambers), which lock users inside information ecosystems, confirming their existing beliefs and worldviews (Pariser, 2011). By systematically suppressing opposing or divergent points of view, algorithmic curation of content erodes the space for critical reflection and public discussion, key prerequisites for a healthy democratic society. The result is social fragmentation and increased polarization, where the common ontological basis for dialogue is gradually disappearing. The price of universal connection, apart from social and political, is also paid on a deeply personal, psychological level. Constant exposure to idealized depictions of other people’s lives on social networks creates fertile ground for social comparison, which often results in feelings of inadequacy, anxiety and depression. The imperative of constant availability and participation in the digital sphere blurs the lines between work and leisure, public and private, creating pressures that negatively impact mental health and general well-being. The role of the digital agent – whether it is a platform, an algorithm or an interface – is crucial in this ecosystem. Its goals, focused primarily on economic metrics such as retention and increased engagement, are often in direct conflict with the long-term interests and well-being of users. Therefore, facing the shadows of digital Eden requires the development of advanced digital literacy, strengthening awareness of the mechanisms that shape our online experience, and the establishment of solid regulatory frameworks that will protect the autonomy, privacy and dignity of the individual in the new digital age.

Figure 2.36: Schematic representation of the psychological cost of universal connectedness: social comparison, anxiety, blurred boundaries between work and rest, and the pressure of constant availability.

2.8 Beginnings of autonomous communication: the first digital interlocutors

The thought of creating artificial beings capable of conversation reaches deep into the human past, from mythical statues that come to life to the Golems of Prague legends. But it was only in the second half of the twentieth century, with the advent of computers, that this age-old aspiration began to take its first real, albeit rudimentary, forms. The transition from myth to technology was conditioned by a key theoretical shift offered by Alan Turing. In his famous work Computing Machinery and Intelligence (Turing, 1950), he did not ask whether machines can think, but whether they can behave in a way that is indistinguishable from humans. His thought experiment, known as the Turing test or the imitation game, established the philosophical and practical framework within which the field of artificial intelligence, and especially the field of natural language processing, would develop for decades. It was the challenge of creating a machine that could successfully conduct a written conversation with a human that became the driving force behind the development of the first digital interlocutors. The first significant step on this path was taken by Joseph Weizenbaum, who created the ELIZA program in 1966. Acting on the principle of recognizing key words and applying simple transformation rules, ELIZA simulated a conversation. Her most famous script, called DOCTOR, imitated a Rogerian psychotherapist, using the technique of paraphrasing and asking open-ended questions taken from user input. For example, the program could respond to the statement “My family worries me” with “Tell me more about your family”. Although technically simple, ELIZA caused an unexpectedly strong reaction. Users credited the program with understanding, empathy, and awareness, despite Weizenbaum’s repeated claims that the machine understood nothing. This phenomenon, which he called the “ELIZA effect”, revealed a deep human tendency to anthropomorphize and establish an emotional connection with even the simplest interlocutor, which deeply worried the author himself and prompted him to critically review the ethical limits of artificial intelligence (Weizenbaum, 1976).

Figure 2.37: Evolutionary steps of the first systems for language interaction: from ELIZE (1966) through PARRY (1972) and SHRDLU (1972) to the further development of dialogic agents and natural language processing.

Shortly after ELIZA, psychiatrist Kenneth Colby from Stanford University developed the PARRY program in 1972. Unlike Weizenbaum’s passive interlocutor, PARRY was designed as a more complex simulation, embodying the personality of a patient with paranoid schizophrenia. Colby’s agent responded to stimuli, but also possessed an internal model of his own beliefs and affective states, such as fear, anger, and distrust, which influenced his responses. PARRY monitored the level of these affects and could proactively change the subject or become defensive if he felt the interlocutor was provoking him. In a series of tests, psychiatrists were often unable to distinguish transcripts of conversations with PARRY from those with human patients. As a historical curiosity, the conversation held in 1972 between ELIZA and PARRY over the ARPANET network, which clearly showed the limitations of both systems - the meeting of the passive mirror and the obsessive model resulted in a mostly incoherent and repetitive exchange. At the same time, a different approach was developed, which was not aimed at simulating the human personality, but at the true understanding of the language within the given context. The most prominent example of such an approach was Terry Winograd’s SHRDLU (1972). This system allowed the user to use natural language to issue commands to a virtual robotic arm in a “cube world”. SHRDLU could understand complex and even ambiguous sentences, ask questions for clarification and remember the context of the conversation. For example, on the command “Pick up the big red cube” the system would execute it. If the user then said “Put it on green”, SHRDLU would correctly understand that the pronoun “is” refers to the aforementioned red cube. Although limited to its microcosm, SHRDLU has shown that a deep understanding of semantics and syntax is possible, steering part of the research community towards knowledge-based models. William Chamberlain and Thomas Etter developed a computer program designed to generate prose and poetry in English (Chamberlain & Etter, 1984). Racter, whose name comes from the word “raconteur” (storyteller), is said to have created the book The Policeman’s Beard Is Half Constructed (published in 1984). According to the editorial framework of that publication, the text was presented as computer-generated, with minimal subsequent interventions, and the system used the rules of context-free grammar and elements of randomness to construct unique sentences and prose (Chamberlain & Etter, 1984; Adamopoulou & Mousiades, 2020). The early systems, from ELIZA to PARRY and SHRDLU, seem technically naive from today’s point of view, but their importance lies in the fact that they showed that machine processing of language was possible. They unraveled the psychological aspects of human-machine interaction and raised fundamental questions about the nature of intelligence, understanding and communication. These were the first, necessary steps in the dark, which, despite their obvious limitations, paved the way towards significantly more complex architectures and paradigms that will mark the next chapter – the world of large language models.

3. The world of large language models: from theory to technology

Figure 3.1: Presentation of the transition from sign to vector representation of language (tokenization, embedding).

3.1 From sign to vector: A paradigmatic shift in the representation of meaning

Observing the development of computer language processing necessarily leads us to observe a thorough transformation in the very theoretical origins of this skill. Classical approaches, which formed the backbone of Natural Language Processing (NLP) for decades, viewed language primarily as a system of arbitrary signs organized according to complex but comprehensible rules. Their starting point was deeply rooted in structural linguistics, and their goal was to impose a formal linguistic order on raw, unstructured text.

This procedure, which can be called a standard pipeline (standard pipeline), consisted of a series of carefully elaborated steps, each of which aims at further normalization and breakdown of the linguistic structure (Jurafsky & Martin, 2023). The first step was regularly tokenization, a process by which an unbroken string of characters is broken down into basic units – tokens – which most often correspond to words and punctuation marks. This was followed by lemmatization, a complex process of reducing a single word to its canonical, dictionary form or lemma. Thus, for example, the forms running, running, running would be reduced to their common lemma running. This put an end to the morphological diversity that hides the fundamental lexical relations. Furthermore, part-of-speech tagging was applied, where each token would be associated with its grammatical identity: noun, verb, adjective and so on. In many applications, such as thematic modeling, the removal of so-called stop words (stop words) - frequent but semantically weak words like conjunctions and prepositions - was carried out.

Token: The smallest unit of text processed by the language model; can match a whole word, a part of a word (subword) or a punctuation mark. Tokenization converts raw text into a string of tokens according to a model dictionary.

The outcome of such analysis was a highly structured, but also an impoverished presentation of the text. It was reduced to a list of lemmas with associated grammatical markers, the so-called “bag of words” (bag of words), which broke the original syntactic structure, and thus a large part of the contextual meaning. Although these procedures were indispensable for the development of early applications, such as spell checkers or simple search systems, their essential limitation became more and more obvious: they could not effectively capture and numerically represent the very semantic core of language – a complex and fluid network of meaning relationships.

A true paradigmatic shift occurred with the appearance of distributional semantics and its computer application in the form of vector representations of words, better known as word embeddings. The theoretical origin of this approach is summarized in the famous thought of linguist John Rupert Firth (1957) that the nature of a word is manifested in the society it forms (“You shall know a word by the company it keeps”). Consequently, words are no longer seen as isolated symbols, but their meaning is constituted through the context in which they appear.

Embedding / investment vector: Numerical (vector) representation of a word, sentence or other language segment in a multidimensional space; the position of the vectors reflects semantic similarity – words with similar meanings have close vectors. It is the basis of distributional semantics and internal representations in LLMs. Corpus: A collection of textual (or other linguistic) data on which the language model is learned; includes books, articles, websites and other sources. The quality and representativeness of the corpus directly affects the performance and biases of the model.

Computational models such as Word2Vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) and GloVe (Pennington et al., 2014) operationalized that insight. Analyzing huge text corpora, these algorithms learned to associate each word with a unique numerical vector in a dense, multidimensional space. The position of each vector is not arbitrary, but is determined by its relationship to all other vectors. Words that appear in similar contexts, such as cat and dog, will have vectors that are close in that space. The word car, which occurs in completely different contexts, will be represented by a vector that is distant from them.

Moreover, relationships between vectors can include more complex semantic analogies. For example, the vector operation VECTOR(“king”) - VECTOR(“man”) + VECTOR(“woman”) results in a vector that is in the immediate vicinity of VECTOR(“queen”). This shows that the model has not only learned mere similarity, but also the fundamental relations that structure our conceptual world.

The transition from symbolic to distributional, vector representation of language was therefore crucial. He enabled computers to represent meaning, that most elusive component of language, in a way that is mathematically tractable and robust. Instead of relying on predefined vocabularies and rigid grammar rules, models could now learn semantic relationships directly from language usage. This opens the way for solving significantly more complex tasks, from a nuanced sentiment analysis to the creation of coherent and contextually appropriate text. Vector representations of words have thus become an indispensable cornerstone on which the entire architecture of contemporary large linguistic models, and thus also the communication agents that are the subject of this book, is built.

Figure 3.2: Meaning as space – from static vectors to dynamic context (transformer, attention).

3.2 Meaning as space: From static vectors to dynamic context

The importance of the transition to vector representation of language cannot be emphasized enough. This cognitive turn made it possible to translate the abstract and fluid concept of meaning into a mathematically comprehensible form.
