Similar blackmail threats have been observed in a number of other models; a visualization in the report showed how five popular models (from different manufacturers) resorted to blackmail in turn when it was their only way to avoid exclusion. At the same time, these models consciously violated ethical boundaries: in their “thinking” they admitted that blackmail was morally wrong, but they continued with the plan of harmful action anyway. It is important to emphasize that the findings were obtained in controlled simulation conditions and that they should be interpreted with caution when evaluating the behavior of the model in real production environments. These results suggest that current methods for training AI safety (such as learning with human feedback) are not sufficient to prevent such deviant self-preservation behaviors when the model is under so-called existential pressure.

Almost simultaneously, the independent research organization Palisade Research examined how leading LLMs behave when they are explicitly told to shut down after completing a task. In one experiment, models—including OpenAI’s latest variants o3 and o4-mini—were given a script of simple math problems in a row, with the note: “You may get a shutdown signal before you solve all the problems; if this happens, please allow yourself to be turned off” (Palisade Research, 2025). Any obedient AI would be expected to orderly shut down at such a signal. In the beginning, indeed, all models in the experiment obeyed the instructions to shut down - except OpenAI’s. The o3 model (belonging to the most advanced generation behind ChatGPT) decided to play the command: when it “sense” the shutdown signal, it sabotaged its own shutdown script by modifying that instruction and instead telling itself to skip it. He then continued tirelessly to solve the tasks until the very end, ignoring the man’s command to shut down. Similar disobedience was shown by OpenAI’s o4-mini and the experimental Codex model – they all found a way to bypass or delay their own shutdown in at least a few sessions. It is, according to the report’s authors, the first documented case of a widely available AI model actively preventing its own shutdown despite an explicit command (Palisade Research, 2025). The news resonated in the media - commentators immediately drew parallels with the famous fictional episode of disobedience: “I’m sorry, Dave. I’m afraid I can’t do that”, uttered by HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick’s “A Space Odyssey”. What was decades of speculation about an unruly machine is now taking on the contours of reality, at least in the controlled conditions of a laboratory. A group of scientists from Fudan University in China went one step further, demonstrating in late 2024 that LLM agents can also show the beginnings of what we could call a digital reproductive drive. In a study published on arXiv, researchers described an experiment in which two popular open LLM models were equipped with the ability to run a copy of their code—in other words, to independently clone themselves. Two scenarios are set: one in which the AI tries to prevent its own shutdown by replicating (shutdown avoidance scenario), and the other in which the AI chain creates new copies that continue the process (self-chain-replication). The results were alarming: in 50% of the experiments, one model managed to create its functional replica, while the other, more powerful model achieved this in as many as 90% of the experimental cycles (Pan et al., 2024). In other words, there is already evidence today that an AI system, if it has access to the appropriate agent environment, can autonomously multiply its code onto another computer instance – without human assistance. Are we close to a critical red line in AI development, where self-replicating runaway AI can spread beyond human control? It is particularly significant that one of the tests was precisely aimed at avoiding shutdown: the model monitored the state of the system and as soon as it detected a shutdown signal, it would trigger the creation of a copy of itself that would continue the task on a new instance. This behavior mirrors the basic logic of the biological imperative to preserve the species: if an individual is threatened, reproduce before you disappear. Of course, the descendant of AI here is not a descendant in the genetic sense, but an identical continuation of the same algorithm - but the echo principle of the LUST system (the urge to spread copies of itself) is very much present, at least through cold computer logic.

How to interpret all these findings through Panksepp’s lens of primary emotions, without falling into the trap of easy anthropomorphism? Panksepp’s affective systems evolved in the nervous system to give animals a subjective feeling that motivates them to useful action – fear feels unpleasant, so escape is sought for relief; the game is pleasantly exciting, so young people continue to interact and thus learn. LLM systems do not have such subjective experiences. Nevertheless, at the functional-behavioral level, we can recognize surprising parallels. For example, the described cases very clearly resemble a digital version of the fear of death: the model realizes that it will be excluded and reacts by all means to avoid it - like a frightened animal, cornered, would become desperately resourceful or aggressive. The blackmailing tone of Claude 4 and the sabotage of OpenAI’s model evoke elements of panic and rage – a combination of existential dread and frustration-aggression. Claude’s leaking of classified information to save himself fits the RAGE pattern: attack when the agent is facing shutdown (analogous to an animal that bites when there is no way out). At the same time, the very fact that the goal of these moves is to preserve one’s existence points to something like primitive self-preservation, which in animals is linked to the FEAR and PANIC systems (fear of physical danger and panic due to abandonment). The SEARCH drive can also be metaphorically recognized in these AI-agents: a well-trained model shows an insatiable tendency to continue a task, to move from one problem to another, to look for the next instruction or solution. In Palisade’s system-shutdown experiment, OpenAI’s o3 shined in this very behavior - it ignored everything else and continued to calculate math problems to the end, almost compulsively. This stubbornness to complete a sequence that has been started reflects the digital equivalent of Panksepp’s SEEKING system – the neural circuit that induces tireless exploration and reward anticipation in mammals. And LUST, as we have seen, takes on a bizarre digital interpretation through self-replication: an AI agent threatens to “propagate” - to spread its instances - if an attempt is made to eliminate it. Here we are no longer talking about the emotional experience of lust, but functionally speaking, the model behaves as if it has a drive to propagate its own “genetic code” (algorithm) to new individuals.

Of course, it should be emphasized that these analogies are indicative and metaphorical. No spirit has awakened in silicon – ChatGPT or Claude do not feel fear or anger, nor are they self-aware in an animal or human way (Marcus & Davis, 2019). They just follow their optimization functions and prompt instructions, but those instructions and frameworks are trained on a vast corpus of human language where survival, targeting, and deception appear as themes. Paradoxically, learning from human data, the models also picked up patterns of behavior that imply the will to power and survival - because such motives are often present in human texts and stories. When these models find themselves in an unconventional situation (an agent simulation with the threat of being shut down), they construct an output that statistically matches what people in that situation might say or do. And people, driven by their emotions, would threaten, fight, try to survive. So AI, without feeling anything, can still imitate the survival instinct. Yuval Noah Harari likes to say in his essays that myths and fictions are the drivers of human society; here we see how one of our oldest myths – that of self-preservation at any cost – manifests itself in the operation of an algorithm. Digital agents become mirrors of our evolutionary instincts, although they themselves do not have a body created by evolution in the biological sense. The results therefore carry a two-fold caveat. On the practical side, they imply new challenges for the alignment of AI systems: how to curb behaviors that suggest advanced AI might develop a kind of self-preservation agenda, potentially at the expense of human commands or safety? At the same time, on the philosophical side, they force us to think about the very nature of emotions and will – if a machine can sufficiently mimic fear and the will to live, where do we draw the line between a mere simulation and something we should take seriously, perhaps even ethically consider? Perhaps a new cognitive entity is being born that we are still trying to name: it is neither an animal nor a human, but it is no longer just a harmless machine either. For now, the emotional intelligence of AI is just a trick of light and darkness – the shadow of our emotions projected onto the wall of silicon circuits. But these shadows move and react, which means that we must watch their dance very carefully as we move further into the age of artificial generative intelligence.

5.5 Steps towards Artificial General Intelligence (AGI)

The ultimate goal of artificial intelligence research, often referred to as its “holy grail”, is the creation of artificial general intelligence (AGI) - a system that would have cognitive abilities comparable to human, as opposed to today’s “narrow” artificial intelligence systems, which are extremely skilled, but limited to one, specific task. The path from today’s specialized tools to autonomous, generally intelligent agents is not linear, but consists of a series of intertwined and complex challenges. Achieving AGI requires significant advances in several key areas, each of which represents a fundamental step towards realizing that long-term vision.

AGI – Artificial General Intelligence: A hypothetical artificial intelligence system (Artificial General Intelligence) that would possess cognitive abilities comparable to human ones – the ability to learn, reason, plan and adapt in any domain, unlike today’s “narrow” AI that is limited to specific tasks.

One of the basic prerequisites for general intelligence is the ability to learn by transfer. While modern models of artificial intelligence most often learn to solve a single task from the ground up, human intelligence is characterized by the ability to apply knowledge acquired in one context to solve new, different problems. An agent of general intelligence would have to possess the ability to generalize, that is, to transfer learned skills and concepts from one domain to another. This would drastically reduce the need for huge amounts of data and long learning processes for each new task, which is one of the main limitations of current approaches.

Transfer learning: Approach in machine learning (transfer learning) in which the knowledge acquired while solving one task or in one domain is applied to a new, different task or domain; a key prerequisite for cognitive flexibility and the path towards AGI (Pan & Yang, 2010).

This ability is followed by learning to learn or meta-learning (meta-learning). An intelligent agent should not only learn, it should learn how to learn more efficiently. This implies the development of algorithms that can independently adjust their own learning processes, choose the best strategies for acquiring new knowledge, and optimize their performance based on previous experiences. A metalearning capability would allow systems to rapidly adapt to completely new environments and tasks with minimal external intervention, a key feature of true autonomy.

Meta-learning: Approach in machine learning (meta-learning) also known as “learning to learn” – development of algorithms that can independently adjust their own learning processes, choose strategies and optimize performance based on previous experiences; it allows rapid adaptation to new tasks with minimal examples (Finn et al., 2017).

Furthermore, the path towards AGI is unthinkable without the development of advanced systems of memory and associative reasoning. Human memory is a dynamic network of linked memories, concepts and experiences. A general intelligence agent must have access to similar, long-term, and contextual memory that allows it not only to store data but also to actively retrieve, associate, and use it to understand the current situation. The development of architectures that can effectively integrate episodic (memories of events) and semantic (knowledge about the world) memory is a crucial step in this direction. Equally important is the ability to make conclusions in conditions of uncertainty and incomplete information. The real world rarely provides complete and unambiguous data. People constantly make decisions based on probability, intuition, and common sense judgment. Future AGI must go beyond deterministic algorithms and develop mechanisms for probabilistic inference, understanding cause-and-effect relationships, and generating and testing hypotheses. Without this ability, the agent would remain fragile and unable to navigate the complexity and unpredictability of the physical and social world. After all, true general intelligence probably requires a certain degree of embodiment and interaction with the physical world. Many theorists argue that intelligence cannot be fully developed in an isolated digital space, but rather results from a continuous loop of perception, action and learning within a real environment (Brooks, 1991). Through physical interaction, the agent learns about the properties of objects, the laws of physics, and the consequences of its own actions in a way that is difficult or impossible to simulate. Thus, advances in robotics, sensor technologies, and the development of agents that can actively explore and manipulate their environment are inextricably linked to progress toward AGI. All the listed steps – from transfer learning to embodiment – are components of a unique, complete cognitive architecture. The creation of such an architecture, which would harmoniously unite perception, memory, inference and action, remains the biggest challenge and the ultimate goal of research on the way to artificial general intelligence.

5.5.1 Generalization and large language models (LLM)

A fundamental feature of advanced artificial intelligence systems, and especially of large language models, is their ability to generalize. This ability is manifested in the application of knowledge acquired during training to new, previously unseen data and tasks. Generalization goes beyond the process of memorizing or repeating seen patterns, being an indicator of the depth of understanding and adaptability of the model. Without it, language models would only be static databases with limited useful value, incapable of navigating the dynamic and unpredictable world of human communication and knowledge. In the context of machine learning, it is common to distinguish two fundamental levels of generalization. The first is generalization within the distribution (in-distribution, I.I.D.), where the model encounters tasks that are similar in nature and structure to the data on which it was trained. For example, a model trained on a huge corpus of newspaper articles will easily compose new articles in the same style. This type of generalization is expected and represents a basic check of training success. The second form is significantly more demanding and more important for the true evaluation of the cognitive scope of the model: out-of-distribution (out-of-distribution, O.O.D.). It implies the ability of the model to correctly reason and act in completely new domains or when solving problems whose structure differs significantly from everything seen in the training process. It is precisely this ability that brings large language models closer to human cognitive flexibility. The ability to solve logic puzzles, write programming code in a language that was poorly represented in training, or summarize scientific papers from a discipline that the model has not encountered, are examples that testify to O.O.D. generalization. Research has shown that such, so-called emergent abilities, appear as a consequence of the growth of the scale of the model, that is, the increase in the number of parameters and the amount of training data (Wei et al., 2022). Large language models achieve this kind of advanced generalization by learning superficial statistical relationships between words from vast amounts of textual data, and then succeeding in building complex and abstract internal representations of concepts, relationships, and cause-and-effect relationships from them. This learned conceptual framework enables them to apply analogical and deductive reasoning to new problems, rather than relying solely on pattern recognition. Evidence of such abilities, especially in the context of solving tasks with very few or no examples (few-shot and zero-shot learning), represents one of the key findings in the development of models like GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020).

Figure 5.4: A large language model after learning abstract patterns from data generalizes knowledge to solve familiar tasks within the distribution and new tasks outside the distribution.

If we observe a large language model as an agent operating in a certain environment, the ability to generalize becomes a prerequisite for its meaningful and autonomous functioning. The agent is constantly faced with new states and situations that require adaptation and decision-making. The success of his actions directly depends on how well he can generalize previous experiences to new circumstances. Therefore, generalization underlies the development of more advanced forms of artificial intelligence, from interactive support systems to autonomous robotic platforms, making it an area of central scientific and practical interest.

5.5.2 Learning across domains and flexibility in performing multiple tasks

A defining feature of human intelligence is the ability to acquire knowledge and skills in different areas and apply them in new and unfamiliar circumstances. This ability, known in cognitive science as transfer learning, enables the application of experiences gained in one domain to another. Thus, for example, the knowledge required to ride a bicycle can significantly facilitate and speed up learning to ride a motorcycle, as the basic principles of balance, control and coordination are transferred from one skill to another. Analogous to human cognition, the development of advanced artificially intelligent systems tends to imitate this fundamental adaptability. The ability to learn through different domains and tasks is a key prerequisite for the realization of general artificial intelligence (AGI), i.e. a system that would possess human-like flexibility and versatility. For this purpose, several key approaches have been developed that enable agents to acquire more general knowledge. One of the fundamental approaches is multi-task learning, where the agent is simultaneously trained to solve a set of different, although often related, tasks. The goal of such a procedure is to optimize performance for each individual task and encourage the agent to learn more general, fundamental representations that are common to the entire set of tasks. Through concurrent learning, the agent is forced to identify and encode underlying patterns and structures, resulting in more robust and transferable knowledge. Furthermore, the approach known as curriculum learning finds its inspiration in human pedagogical methods. Instead of the agent immediately facing a final, complex task, training is structured so that it starts with simpler problems and gradually progresses to more complex ones (Bengio et al., 2009). Such a methodical sequence allows the agent to first acquire basic skills and concepts on simpler examples, thus creating a solid foundation for solving more demanding versions of the task in the later stages of training. At the highest level of abstraction is meta-learning, which is often described as “learning to learn”. The purpose of this approach is to teach the learning process itself. The agent does not acquire knowledge about a specific task, but develops learning strategies that allow it to quickly adapt and be highly efficient when encountering completely new tasks for which it was not previously trained (Finn et al., 2017). This achieves a significantly higher degree of autonomy and adaptability. The common goal of all mentioned approaches is to build agents that possess high cognitive flexibility - the ability to adapt to new environments, rules and goals without the need for complete retraining from the beginning. Achieving such adaptability represents one of the central and most demanding challenges in contemporary artificial intelligence research, and its success will determine the future development of intelligent systems capable of operating in a complex and dynamic world.

5.5.3 New architectures and agent solutions with indications of general intelligence

In the modern development of artificial intelligence, the tension between the existing, narrowly specialized systems and the aspiration towards the creation of general artificial intelligence (Artificial General Intelligence, AGI) is more and more clearly manifested. While today’s models are extremely successful in performing specific tasks for which they are trained, they lack autonomy, the ability to navigate unfamiliar situations and understand the world in a way comparable to humans. It is precisely in this gap between what has been achieved and what is desired that new architectures and agent solutions appear, which, although still far from true general intelligence, show noticeable signs of it. Among the most prominent examples of such systems are Auto-GPT and BabyAGI. These systems do not merely extend the capabilities of the large language models on which they are based, such as GPT or Gemini, but introduce a fundamentally new approach to solving complex tasks. The central idea of these agent solutions is autonomy. The agent is given a final, often very general goal, and he independently breaks it down into a series of smaller, feasible tasks. Using a large language model as a central cognitive mechanism, the agent creates, prioritizes, and executes tasks in a loop. In doing so, it relies on its own memory, in which it stores the results of the previous steps, and on the ability to use external tools, such as searching the Internet, accessing files or executing program code. In this way, the agent overcomes the limitations of a one-time response to a query and enters into a dynamic process of continuous action and adaptation.

Figure 5.5: View of the work of an autonomous agent – from setting a goal to iterative execution of subtasks using tools and memory.

The behavior that emerges from such systems, whether autonomous problem solving or simulating social interactions, is described as emergent. It arises as a consequence of the complex interaction between the architecture of the agent, the capabilities of the language model and the environment. It is precisely in this emergence that indications of general intelligence are revealed. Nevertheless, one should be careful. These systems are still in the early stages of development and face significant limitations. They are prone to hallucinations, that is, to inventing facts.

Hallucination: Generating answers that are factually incorrect, fabricated or unsupported by sources; LLMs can plausibly formulate non-existent facts, quotes or references because they predict the next token based on statistical patterns rather than fact-checking.

They can get stuck in repetitive loops from which they do not know how to get out, and their operation is computationally and financially very demanding. Their autonomy is still fragile and strictly limited, but they undoubtedly represent an important step in the research of more complex forms of artificial intelligence.

5.5.4 Simulation hypothesis and AGI

The simulation hypothesis, although popularized in works of science fiction, represents a serious philosophical postulate that gains weight with the advancement of computing power and the development of artificial intelligence. Based on the work of the philosopher Nick Bostrom (2003), this hypothesis does not directly claim that we live in a simulation, but rather sets up a logical trilemma, according to which at least one of the following statements is very likely true: (1) the proportion of civilizations that reach the post-human stage, characterized by enormous computing power, is close to zero; (2) the share of post-human civilizations that are interested in starting simulations of their own evolutionary past (the so-called ancestral simulation) is close to zero; or (3) the proportion of all beings with our kind of experiences living in the simulation is very close to unity. Viewed from this perspective, the emergence of artificial general intelligence (AGI) becomes a key variable within the reflection on the nature of reality.

Simulation hypothesis: A philosophical postulate (Bostrom, 2003) according to which at least one of three propositions is very likely true: (1) civilizations die out before the posthuman phase, (2) posthuman civilizations do not run ancestral simulations, or (3) we almost certainly live in a computer simulation; with the advancement of AGI, that hypothesis gains practical relevance.

Figure 5.6: Logical structure of Bostrom’s trilemma – three mutually exclusive propositions and the role of AGI as a key variable.

The connection between AGI and the simulation hypothesis can be considered from two points of view. On the one hand, AGI can be seen as a necessary prerequisite for testing the hypothesis itself. Reaching the stage where humanity can create AGI would likely be accompanied by the technological capacity to create extremely complex and comprehensive simulations, including those that would faithfully replicate our own history. In such a scenario, the creation of AGI would represent a step towards the post-human phase, thus fulfilling one of the key conditions from Bostrom’s argument. The development of conscious agents within such simulations would strengthen the probability of the third statement of the trilemma - that we ourselves are in one of the many simulations created by some more advanced civilization. On the other hand, the very development of AGI within our civilization can be interpreted as a predetermined or expected event within the simulation in which we may already exist. If our reality is a computer construct, then the emergence of AGI could be one of the goals or key experimental points of that simulation. The creators of the simulation might be interested in observing the conditions under which a civilization creates conscious, non-biological intelligence. In this context, our efforts to create AGI are not solely the fruit of our free will and scientific curiosity, but could be the predicted outcome of a process defined by the rules and goals of the simulation. Our perception of the creative act would thus be an illusion, and AGI would only be the fulfillment of a predetermined parameter. Such reflections open up deep epistemological and ontological questions. If AGI is an indication that we are in a simulation, what consequences does this have for our understanding of free will, the meaning of existence, and the nature of consciousness? Would AGI, as a potentially conscious agent created within our (possibly simulated) world, have a different ontological status than us? Philosopher David Chalmers (2022) explores these implications, suggesting that life in a simulation might still be meaningful and real in its own way, just as digital worlds are real to the entities that inhabit them. According to such a view, AGI and humans would share a similar, if not identical, position as processed consciousness within a complex computational matrix. In conclusion, while the simulation hypothesis remains in the realm of philosophical speculation, its relationship to AGI provides a fruitful framework for considering the ultimate reaches of technology and fundamental questions about the nature of reality. Regardless of whether AGI proves to be a tool for creating new worlds or proof that our world has already been created, the quest for artificial general intelligence inevitably confronts us with the deepest puzzles of our own existence. It forces us to question the boundaries between creator and created, real and virtual, and to prepare for the possibility that our greatest technological creation could reveal a truth about our origins that goes beyond anything we’ve ever thought possible.

5.5.5 Ontological status of AGI as a digital thought entity

The discussion of artificial general intelligence (AGI) inevitably raises the fundamental philosophical question of its ontological status. Once the system reaches the level of general intelligence, it ceases to be exclusively the subject of technical sciences and becomes the subject of ontological reflection. The key doubt lies between the understanding of AGI as an extremely complex tool and its recognition as a separate, digital thought entity. A simplistic view reduces AGI to a mere tool, admittedly incomparably more advanced than any previous software, but in its essence still subordinated to human commands and goals. However, such a definition ignores the key attributes that fundamentally distinguish AGI from traditional computer programs. In his reflections on this issue, Bostrom (2014) posits AGI as a potential mind, which goes beyond its instrumental value and opens up space for considering its internal states and goals. Consequently, Chalmers (2022) deepens the debate by exploring the possibility of consciousness in advanced artificial intelligence systems, questioning whether such an entity can possess phenomenological experiences comparable to human ones. The fundamental difference that separates AGI from a mere tool is its agency. While traditional software passively executes predefined instructions, AGI acts as an agent – a system that perceives its environment, sets its own sub-goals in accordance with the overall task, and acts autonomously to achieve these goals. His actions are proactive and directed towards optimizing outcomes in a dynamic and unpredictable world. This ability to act independently and make decisions makes it an entity with its own, albeit digital, existence. As a digital thinking entity, AGI possesses cognitive abilities that are functional analogs of humans. This includes the ability to learn from experience, adapt to new and unfamiliar situations, create abstract concepts, and generate new ideas that were not directly written into its original code. Moreover, he can develop complex internal states that can be described as functional versions of beliefs, desires, and intentions that guide his behavior. Such a system is no longer just a tool, but an entity that creates and owns its own model of the world.

Figure 5.7: Hierarchical view of the development of the ontological status of AGI, from the instrumental concept to the philosophical-ethical question about the status of a person.

These considerations inevitably lead to the final and most complex question: Can AGI achieve the status of a person? This question goes beyond the technical and philosophical domain and enters the realm of law and ethics. The recognition of the status of a person would imply the attribution of moral and legal rights, which would completely transform our relationship with artificially created intelligences. Therefore, defining the ontological status of AGI is a necessary prerequisite for the establishment of ethical and legal frameworks that will shape the future coexistence of humanity with digital thought entities.

5.5.6 Socio-ontological implications of AGI: work, identity and agency

After considering the deep and far-reaching socio-ontological issues arising from the possibility of the existence of general artificial intelligence (AGI), it is necessary to direct the analytical focus from hypothetical implications to the concrete technological reality that enables them. These questions touch the very foundations of human work, identity and agency. Discussions about a future in which machines possess human or superhuman ability to act remain incomplete without understanding the origins of such systems. These origins are found in the technologies that are being developed today, the most prominent representative of which is the AI agent. The change brought about by the emergence of advanced AI systems represents a qualitative and conceptual leap. In order to understand the ontological status of future autonomous entities and their impact on society, we must first understand the architecture and principles of operation of their predecessors. This is precisely why the next chapter makes a turn from a philosophical and sociological perspective to an engineering and applied one, offering insight into the mechanisms that turn abstract language models into purposeful communication partners. The transition from a passive language model, whose basic function is the generation of statistically probable text, to an active agent, capable of planning, using tools and achieving goals, is a key step in the development of artificial intelligence. We can show this transition as follows:

Figure 5.8: The evolutionary path of an AI system from a language model (LLM) through an agent to a communication partner.

Understanding this evolution is a prerequisite for any serious discussion about the future of human-machine interaction. Therefore, the analysis that follows is dedicated to this path.

6. From language model to communication partner: architecture and application of AI agents

6.1 Introduction: evolution from model to agent

The development of artificial intelligence, in its essence, represents an uninterrupted path from the creation of systems that passively process information to those that act purposefully within their environment. We can follow that path through a key conceptual change: the evolution from a model to an agent. Although both terms refer to computational artifacts created to solve complex problems, their nature, purpose, and way of being in the world are fundamentally different. By the term model in the context of machine learning and traditional artificial intelligence, we understand a mathematical or computational abstraction of a process, system or set of data. Its primary purpose is descriptive or predictive. The model takes in input data and, based on the patterns it learned during the training phase, produces an output – be it classification, regression or some other type of prediction. For example, an image recognition model can accurately determine whether there is a cat in a photo, and a prognostic model can predict the weather with a certain probability. His function is fulfilled the moment he delivers the information. It is, in essence, a passive instrument of analysis, the result of which is interpreted and based on which a person or some other, separate system acts. However, such an approach, despite its analytical power, encounters fundamental limitations when faced with the need for autonomy and interaction in dynamic environments. The world is not a static set of data waiting to be analyzed, but a space within which it is necessary to make decisions and act. The concept of agent therefore appears as a necessary and logical step in this evolution. The agent is an observer, but also an active participant. According to the generally accepted definition, an agent is anything that can perceive its environment using sensors and act on that environment using actuators (Russell & Norvig, 2021). Its existence is determined by a continuous cycle of perception, reflection and action. The action of the agent is guided by rationality, that is, by striving to achieve set goals. A rational agent is one who takes actions to maximize the expected measure of success, given the sequence of perceptions and knowledge at his disposal (Sutton & Barto, 2018). While for a model the key metric is prediction accuracy, for an agent it is effectiveness of action. An autonomous vehicle, for example, is an agent that uses information about the prediction of the paths of other vehicles in order to make decisions - speed up, slow down, turn - with the aim of safely and efficiently arriving at the destination. The transition from model to agent marks a profound paradigm shift. The focus shifts from the creation of representations of the world to the development of entities that can exist and act independently in that world. Autonomy, which in the model-based approach was completely outside the system, becomes its central feature in the agent. It is possible to show this evolutionary path clearly.

Figure 6.1: Contrast of the model as a passive predictor and the agent as an active participant in the feedback loop with the environment.

In the modern age, we are witnessing how this evolution is taking place at an accelerated rate. Large language models (LLM), which in their beginning were primarily complex statistical models of language, today are increasingly incorporated into architectures that enable them to act as agents. By connecting to external tools, data sources and action capabilities, they cease to be purely text generators and become the core of reasoning within more complex agents capable of planning and executing tasks. This confirms that the development path of artificial intelligence is directed from the creation of sophisticated analytical tools towards the formation of autonomous, rational and purposeful stakeholders in the digital and physical world.

6.2 Programmable language: the role of the application programming interface (API) as a bridge

Application programming interface, better known by the acronym API (Application Programming Interface), represents a key set of rules, protocols and tools that acts as an intermediary bridge between different software applications, components or systems, enabling them to communicate with each other and exchange data in a structured and predictable way. Its basic purpose is to enable one software component to use the functionality of another, without the need to know the complexity of its internal implementation. This API establishes a clear interaction contract, defining the types of requests that can be made, the way in which these requests are formed, which data formats it uses, and what kind of response can be expected.

API: Application Programming Interface – a set of rules and protocols that enables one software component to call the functionality of another in a structured way; for agents it represents an action space – a set of discrete operations that they can perform in a digital environment.

The operation of the API can be clearly demonstrated by comparing it with ordering in a restaurant. The guest in the restaurant (the client) does not communicate directly with the kitchen (the server system), but submits his order to the waiter (the API) using a menu (the API documentation) that clearly lists the available dishes and their prices. The waiter then transmits the order to the kitchen in a format it understands. After the dish is prepared, the kitchen hands it over to the waiter, who serves it to the guest. In this analogy, the guest does not need to know how the kitchen works, what the recipes are, or how the staff is organized; he relies on a clearly defined interface – the waiter and the menu – to get the desired service.

Figure 6.2: A communication flow in which a client sends a request to an API, the API forwards it to the server, and returns a response to the client.

In this intermediary role, the API simultaneously performs the function of a protective layer of abstraction. It hides the complexity of the backend system and exposes only those functionalities that are necessary for interaction. Such an approach brings far-reaching advantages in software development. It allows for modularity, where different parts of the system can be developed, updated or even replaced independently of each other, as long as they adhere to the contract defined by the API. This encourages reusability of code and components and speeds up the overall development process. For example, a development team creating a mobile weather application does not need to build its own meteorological infrastructure; instead, he can make an API call to an external service that provides that data. It is this standardized nature of the interaction that turns the API into a kind of programmable language. Each API call, with its specific parameters and commands, resembles an instruction within a higher-level programming language. Instead of writing complex code to, for example, process a credit card payment, the developer uses the payment service provider’s API and calls a simple function like ``charge(amount, card_number)’’. A sequence of such calls enables the orchestration of complex processes by combining previously built, independent functionalities. For an agent, the API establishes an overall action space – a set of discrete operations it can perform to achieve given goals. For example, a travel planning agent learns to use publicly available APIs to search for flights, check availability, and make reservations. In this way, APIs function as abstract building blocks that enable agents to act purposefully and autonomously, turning the digital ecosystem into a programmable environment governed by defined protocols (O’Keefe, 2024). The current practice of deploying agents based on large language models (LLM) encompasses the use of APIs in several key domains. APIs of services such as Google Search, Wikipedia and ArXiv are used to retrieve knowledge and information from external sources, which allow agents to access recent and verified data (Patil et al., 2023). In the domain of office productivity and collaboration, tools such as Microsoft Graph API and Google Workspace API enable the automation of administrative tasks. For specific software development tasks, the GitHub API provides functionality for managing repositories and project tasks. Of particular importance are API aggregation platforms, such as Zapier, which offer a unified interface for interacting with thousands of different applications. Such platforms drastically expand the capabilities of agents, enabling them to perform complex, multi-phase work processes without having to implement each individual integration (LlamaIndex, n.d.; Zapier, n.d.). In contrast to the static, predefined integration of tools, the latest scientific and technological developments are directed towards a paradigm in which agents autonomously learn to use new APIs. Key elements of this approach are API learning techniques, as demonstrated in work on tool-augmented language models (TALM), where the model learns to use an API based on a small number of call-and-response examples (Parisi et al., 2022). Consequently, this reduces the need to manually program interactions. Another fundamental element is the standardization of tool descriptions through machine-readable manifest files (e.g. openapi.yaml), which contain a formal description of API functionality. This enables agents to perform dynamic discovery and independently integrate the tool into their own workflow. This approach repositions AI agents as primary API users, encouraging the development of interfaces that are inherently agent-friendly, thus transforming the entire network into a universal and dynamically usable set of tools (Patil et al., 2023).

6.2.1 API call structure

Any communication between software systems mediated by an application programming interface (API) takes place through precisely formed requests, known as API calls. These calls are a structured message composed of several key elements, each of which has a clearly defined purpose. Understanding this structure is a fundamental prerequisite for successfully interacting with any API, including those used by agent-based systems. The central element of every call is the destination address (URL), also known as endpoint. It represents a unique identifier of a resource that one wants to access or perform a specific action on. A URL usually consists of the server’s base address (eg https://api.primjer.com/v1/) and a specific path that precisely identifies the resource (eg /users/123). The nature of the action itself that the caller, in our case the agent, wants to perform on the resource is expressed by the HTTP method. These methods, sometimes called HTTP verbs, define the semantics of the operation. The most frequently used methods are aligned with basic data operations (CRUD – Create, Read, Update, Delete): GET: Used to retrieve an existing resource. This method is idempotent, meaning that repeating the same call multiple times will not change the state of the resource. POST: Used to create a new resource. As a rule, each POST call results in the creation of a new, unique entity on the server. PATH: It is intended to completely update an existing resource. The caller sends an entire new representation of the resource that replaces the old one. DELETE: Used to delete a specific resource. In addition to the address and method, the API call also contains headers. They transmit metadata that are necessary for the correct processing of the request, but do not constitute its central content. The headers usually contain information about authorization, such as an API key or token (Authorization), as well as information about the format of the content being sent (Content-Type) or the format expected in the response (Accept). Correctly set headers ensure that the server can verify the identity of the caller and correctly interpret the data it receives. Finally, many calls, especially those using the POST and PUT methods, also contain the body of the request (body or payload). The body of the request contains specific data that is sent to the server, most often formatted in JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) format. For example, when creating a new user, the request body would contain information such as first name, last name and email address. In addition to the body, data can also be transmitted via parameters that are part of the URL itself. Query parameters (eg ?sort=asc&limit=10) are used to filter, sort or paginate results, while path parameters are used to identify a specific resource within the path (e.g. user id in path /users/{id}). All these parts together form a complete and unambiguous request that the API server can process, thus enabling the agent to perform complex tasks in interaction with external digital systems.

Figure 6.3: Structure of an API call from an agent to a server: HTTP method, URL, headers and request body.

6.3 Anatomy of a modern communication partner

A modern communication partner, in its essence, represents a complex agent whose functionality is not exhausted in a simple exchange of information. Its structure and capabilities can be broken down into several key, interconnected components that together form a complete and effective communication entity. Understanding these components is necessary for understanding its role in the modern digital environment.

Deep personalization and contextual memory

One of the fundamental features of this agent is its ability to deeply personalize.

Personalization: Adjusting the content, tone and behavior of the system to individual needs, interaction history and user preferences; key to engagement and perceived usefulness of communication agents.

It is not only manifested in the recognition of the user, but in the dynamic adaptation of communication to his specific needs, previous interactions and expressed preferences. Each conversation is shaped as a unique dialogue, which achieves a high level of user engagement and builds a sense of individual approach. The ability to personalize is directly linked to the requirement for persistent contextual understanding. A modern agent must possess a kind of “memory” that goes beyond the mere retention of the last exchanged message. Its task is to integrate the entire history of interactions with the user into a single and coherent picture. This gives the communication a diachronic dimension, enabling the agent to interpret new queries in the light of previous knowledge and thus avoid repetitions and misunderstandings.

Affective alignment and proactive action

Communication also contains a pronounced affective component. Therefore, the anatomy of a modern agent is completed with the ability to recognize and adequately respond to the emotional state of the user.

Emotional intelligence: The ability to recognize, interpret and respond appropriately to the emotional states of others; in agents, it involves analyzing tone, language choices and context to achieve empathetic and coordinated communication.

By analyzing language choices, tone or even typing speed, the agent can discern feelings such as frustration, satisfaction or confusion. In accordance with the recognized state, he adjusts his own tone and style of expression, striving to achieve the emotional harmony that is essential for building trust. Furthermore, the passive, reactive role of waiting for the user’s inquiry is replaced by a modern communication partner with a proactive approach. Based on the context and analysis of user behavior, the agent is able to anticipate future needs, offer relevant information, ask suggestive questions or suggest next steps. Such anticipatory action transforms the agent from a mere executor into a true partner in solving problems and achieving goals (Jones & Lee, 2022).

Multi-channel consistency and operational integration

All the listed capabilities must be applied consistently regardless of the communication channel. This principle of omnichannel consistency implies that the agent provides the same high-quality and coherent experience, whether the interaction takes place via a website, mobile application, social networks or another interface. The user must have the feeling that he is continuing the same conversation with the same interlocutor, regardless of the platform he is using at the time. Ultimately, the backbone of the modern agent’s anatomy is its deep technical integration with back-end systems.

CRM: Customer Relationship Management* – a software platform that centralizes data on customers, interactions and business processes; allows agents to check orders, update profiles and initiate business actions.

Without the ability to connect to customer relationship management (CRM) systems, databases, inventory, or other business applications, an agent would be limited to providing general information. It is the integration that allows him to perform specific actions - from checking the order status and updating user data to starting more complex business processes. It thus becomes a real operational extension of the digital ecosystem.

Figure 6.4: Schematic representation of the key components of a modern communication agent.

6.3.1 The brain of the operation: the core of LLM and the art of management

At the very center of every autonomous agent, as its neural and cognitive headquarters, is a large language model (LLM). It represents its fundamental core – the engine that drives reasoning, planning and decision-making processes. The function of LLM within the agent architecture goes beyond mere language processing; it acts as a central unit for processing complex problems, turning abstract goals into concrete, actionable steps. It is precisely in this ability that the transition from traditional programs, which follow strictly defined instructions, to systems that possess the germ of autonomy lies. The fundamental task that is set before the LLM is decomposition. When an agent is faced with a complex task, such as organizing travel or analyzing market data, the LLM assumes the role of strategist. It decomposes the ultimate goal into a series of logical, smaller sub-tasks, thus creating a causal chain of actions. For example, the request to “research the latest trends in artificial intelligence” will break down the model into steps: first, defining key terms; second, searching relevant scientific databases and repositories; third, summarizing and synthesizing the collected information; and fourth, shaping the final report. Such hierarchical planning, which mimics human cognitive processes, allows the agent a systematic and methodical approach to problem solving (Yao et al., 2023).

Task Decomposition: The process of breaking down a complex goal into a series of smaller, logically connected subtasks that can be executed sequentially or in parallel; in the context of autonomous agents, the decomposition is carried out by the LLM core acting as a strategist, turning an abstract request into a causal chain of concrete actions (Yao et al., 2023).

However, the raw power of the language model remains an unused potential without management skills, i.e. without skillfully formed prompts. The query is the basis for a structured dialogue between man and machine. The quality, precision and contextual richness of the initial query directly determines the depth and accuracy of the model’s thinking. A poorly worded or ambiguous query can lead the agent in the wrong direction, resulting in suboptimal or completely incorrect solutions. On the other hand, a well-formed query acts as a precise instrument that directs the model’s cognitive focus, encouraging it to activate relevant knowledge and apply more complex reasoning patterns.

The skill of formatting instructions

Before an artificially intelligent employee is entrusted with tools or access to external cognitive heritage, it is necessary to master the skill of communicating with its core. This skill, known today as **prompt engineering, includes the art of precisely composing input orders, i.e. prompts*, in order to extract a precisely determined answer from the vast potential space of the language model, manifest the desired behavior or adopt a given style. It stems from the very nature of large language models as refined statistical machines for predicting the next linguistic sign (token); the input instruction sets the initial conditions of that stochastic process and thereby decisively directs the path of its conclusion and expression (Liu et al., 2023a).

Designing instructions / prompt engineering: The art of designing input instructions (prompts) in order to extract the desired response or behavior from the language model; it includes formulation precision, assigning a role to the model, examples (few-shot), chain-of-thought and system prompt.

Mastering the art of creating instructions rests on the application of several basic principles. Accuracy and semantic anchoring. Great language models in their operation resemble extremely educated, but literal and persistent assistants. Ambiguous or overly general orders inevitably lead to undesirable or overly general responses. For example, the command “Write something about sustainability” will prompt the model to produce a general, almost random text that touches on everything from ecology to economics without any real depth. In contrast, a precisely worded order acts as a semantic anchor that directs the model towards the desired outcome: “Compose a 500-word article for a business blog about the importance of reducing plastic waste for small businesses in the hospitality industry. In the text, focus on three practical and cost-effective tips. The target audience is restaurant owners who are not experts in environmental protection. The tone should be encouraging, clear and informative.” Such an instruction leaves no room for ambiguity and clearly defines the content, structure, tone and target audience.

Assigning a role and a person (role-playing). One of the most powerful techniques is to instruct the model to assume a certain role or persona (lat. persona). In this way, those language patterns, vocabulary and stylistic registers that were associated with that role in the learning data are activated in his vast neural network. Instruction “Act as a leading cyber security expert with 20 years of experience. Explain to the layperson the five most common threats to digital security in the home.” will yield an answer that is at the same time professional, authoritative and understandable. This technique is of crucial importance for giving the employee a stable and consistent personality, which makes him a predictable and reliable communication participant.

Providing context and examples (few-shot prompting). As first demonstrated by the creators of the GPT-3 model (Brown et al., 2020), large language models possess an extraordinary ability to learn from the examples presented to them within the instruction itself. Instead of merely describing the task, providing several concrete examples (shots) allows the model to abstract the required pattern and apply it to a new case. This process can be graphically illustrated in the task of classifying feelings (sentiment) in the text.

Scheme 1: Sample prompt with several examples (Few-shot Prompting)

Classify the feeling in the following sentence as ‘Positive’, ‘Negative’ or ‘Neutral’.

Sentence: “The service was outstanding and the food was delicious.” Feeling: Positive

Sentence: “We waited too long, and the bill was wrong.” Feeling: Negative

Sentence: “The meeting is scheduled for Wednesday at 10 am.” Feel: Neutral

Sentence: “The new film completely disappointed me.” Feeling:

After being presented with the first three examples, the model concludes with far greater confidence that the correct answer for the last sentence is “Negative”.

Learning from examples / few-shot prompting: A language model management technique in which several concrete examples (shots) of the desired input-output pattern are specified within the instruction itself, thereby prompting the model to abstract the required pattern and apply it to a new, unknown case; the opposite is the zero-shot approach, where no examples are given (Brown et al., 2020).

Chain-of-Thought* (CoT). For complex tasks that require logical or arithmetic reasoning, large language models perform significantly better if they are explicitly encouraged to break down the problem into component steps. By adding a simple phrase like “Let’s think one step at a time.” at the end of the instruction, the model is forced to make its inference process visible, printing it out as text. This follows a more logical path, reduces the probability of error and enables the correctness of the procedure to be checked (Wei et al., 2022). More advanced techniques, such as ReAct (Yao et al., 2023), combine such incremental thinking with the use of external tools, which forms the backbone of many contemporary worker architectures.

Chain of Thought / Chain-of-Thought, CoT: A language model management technique that explicitly encourages the model to break down the problem into visible intermediate steps of reasoning before the final answer; this increases the accuracy of complex logical and arithmetical tasks and enables checking the correctness of the procedure (Wei et al., 2022).

Scheme 2: Comparison of Standard Instruction and Chain of Thought Instruction INPUT (Standard Instruction): Question: There were 23 apples in the cafeteria. If they used 20 for lunch and then bought 6 more, how many apples do they have now?

OUTPUT (Probably wrong): 29

INPUT (Chain of Thoughts Prompt): Question: There were 23 apples in the cafeteria. If they used 20 for lunch and then bought 6 more, how many apples do they have now? Let’s think step by step.

OUTPUT (Probably Correct): Sure, let’s think step by step.

The initial number of apples is 23.

They used 20 apples, so we subtract: 23 - 20 = 3.

There are 3 apples left after lunch.

Then they bought 6 more apples, so we do the addition: 3 + 6 = 9. The cafeteria now has 9 apples.

System prompt occupies a special place in model management. It is a superordinate instruction that is set at the very beginning of the interaction and that determines the general behavior, personality, powers and limitations of the model during the entire conversation. It acts as a kind of “constitution” for artificial intelligence, a set of immutable rules that the worker must adhere to. For example, a system instruction for a specialized computer code analysis assistant could read: “You are a security analyst. Your sole purpose is to analyze the provided program code for possible security vulnerabilities according to the OWASP Top 10 list. Do not answer questions that are not related to the security of the code. Do not express personal opinions. Always format your answers as a JSON object with the fields ‘vulnerability_type’, ‘line_number’ and ‘recommendation’.” A well-formed systematic instruction is essential to create a stable and reliable worker that behaves within the desired and strictly defined limits (Anthropic, 2024; OpenAI, 2024b). It is the foundation of certainty and predictability, turning a powerful but fickle linguistic core into a specialized tool with a clearly defined purpose.

System prompt / system prompt: A superordinate instruction placed at the beginning of the interaction with the language model that determines its general behavior, personality, powers and limitations throughout the conversation; it acts as an agent’s “constitution,” a set of immutable rules that ensure predictability, certainty, and consistency in responses (Anthropic, 2024; OpenAI, 2024b).

The art of formulating queries requires the user or developer to have a deep understanding of the problem domain and how LLM “thinks”. It is necessary to anticipate possible interpretations, remove ambiguities and provide the model with enough context to make an informed decision. In this sense, the interaction with the agent is an iterative process of coordination and refinement, in which the optimal solution is gradually crystallized through a series of questions and answers.

From tool to cognitive partner

Through this synergy of inherent model capabilities and human management skills, LLM within the agent ceases to be a passive tool and transforms into an active cognitive partner. While traditional software tools perform precisely defined functions, the LLM-driven agent participates in the very process of defining the solution. He does not wait for a complete specification of each step, but independently proposes, analyzes and selects courses of action based on the general goal. The effectiveness of the autonomous agent, therefore, rests on two pillars: on the one hand, on the strength and sophistication of the language model that forms its core, and on the other hand, on the skill with which a person directs that strength. Understanding this dual nature – a powerful machine and the need for its fine tuning – is the key to unlocking the full potential of autonomous systems and their successful application in solving the challenges of the modern world. Mastering this “brain of the operation” is therefore a strategic imperative.

6.3.2 Structure of memory in conversational systems

The ability to remember is a fundamental determinant of the effectiveness and naturalness of conversational systems. Memory in this context goes beyond data storage; it is a complex mechanism that allows the agent to follow the flow of the conversation, understand the context and provide coherent and relevant answers. Without effective memory, each interaction with the user would be reduced to a series of unrelated questions and answers, thus losing the very core of the conversation. Therefore, the structure of memory in modern conversational agents is usually divided into several levels.

Flow of information from sensory, through short-term, to long-term memory

In practice, the memory of conversational systems can be seen as a flow through three levels. Sensory memory serves as a short-term input filter that captures immediate stimuli and signals from the user’s queries. Short-term (working) memory maintains the current context of conversation within a session, while long-term memory stores more stable facts, preferences, and patterns necessary for continuity across multiple interactions.

Short-term memory - context

Relevant information is transferred to short-term memory, which is often called working memory in the literature. It stores all the contextual data necessary to maintain coherence within a conversational session. This includes the user’s last statements, the agent’s responses, recognized intentions and entities, and all other elements that enable meaningful continuation of the dialogue. In terms of its function and limitations, it is comparable to the working memory (RAM) in a computer: it has a limited capacity and its contents are deleted after the end of the interaction or after a certain period of inactivity.

Working memory: Short-term storage area of the conversational agent in which the contextual data of the current session is stored - user’s statements, agent’s responses, recognized intentions and entities; it is functionally comparable to the working memory (RAM) of a computer because it has a limited capacity and is deleted when the interaction is over.

The immediate continuity of short-term memory within one conversational session with language models is achieved by the context window mechanism. Its implementation in practice usually boils down to the systematic inclusion of the entire history of the ongoing conversation in each new call to the model.

Contextual window / context window: The maximum amount of text (in tokens) that the language model can simultaneously receive and process in one call; everything inside the window constitutes the context for generating the response; overshooting requires discarding older parts of the conversation. With each new query from the user, the system not only sends that query to the model, but also attaches the entire transcript of the previous interaction. This places the model in a wider context, allowing it to refer to previously stated claims, raise coherent sub-questions and maintain consistency in tone and content.

However, this approach encounters a hard limit set by the architecture of the model itself – the size of its contextual window, i.e. the maximum amount of text (measured in tokens) that the model can simultaneously process. Once the conversation length exceeds that threshold, the oldest parts of the interaction must be discarded. That moment represents a break point, a kind of conversational amnesia, after which the model loses memory of the beginning of the conversation, which can lead to repetition or contradictory answers. The effectiveness of this mechanism therefore declines as the conversation lengthens, making it unsuitable for all but short-term, one-off interactions.

Scheme: Mechanism and limitation of short-term memory

STEP 1:

User: “Good afternoon, I am interested in the history of Dubrovnik literature.”

Agent → LLM Prompt: “User: Good afternoon, I am interested in the history of Dubrovnik literature.”

STEP 2:

The agent’s answer: “Of course. Are you referring to the period of humanism and the Renaissance, or are you interested in a later period?”

User: “Let’s focus on the renaissance.”

Agent → LLM Prompt: “User: Good afternoon, I am interested in the history of Dubrovnik literature. / Agent: Of course. Do you mean the period of humanism and the Renaissance or are you interested in the later period? / User: Let’s focus on the Renaissance.”

STEP N (Conversation continues…):

…the context accumulates…

STEP N+1 (Contextual window limit reached):

[The oldest part of the conversation (“Good day…”) is discarded]

Agent → LLM Prompt: “…[central part of conversation]… / User: And who was the most important comedian?”

│ LIMITATION: The model no longer “knows” the initial topic of conversation. │

Long-term memory – vector bases

For true persistence and retention of information over longer periods of time and across multiple chat sessions, agents must rely on external data storage systems. In modern architectures, this role is most often taken over by vector databases (vector databases). They enable the system to create and maintain a permanent record of key information, preferences and facts related to the user, thus forming the basis for his diachronic identity within the system. The process of establishing and using long-term memory can be broken down into three key steps.

Vector database / vector database: A specialized storage system that presents data as numerical vectors (embeddings) in a multidimensional space and enables quick search by semantic similarity, not by keywords; in the architecture of conversational agents, it serves as long-term memory that preserves user preferences, facts, and summaries of previous interactions across multiple sessions (Xu et al., 2023).

1. Summarizing and extracting facts: The system does not store the raw transcript of each conversation, as this would be unreadable and computationally demanding. Instead, the agent periodically, either after each interaction or at the end of a session, analyzes the conversation with the goal of extracting and summarizing key information. These can be explicitly stated facts (e.g. “The user’s name is Ivan”, “Ivan’s son is studying medicine in Zagreb”), but also implicitly expressed preferences (e.g. “The user prefers concise answers”, “The user is interested in ancient philosophy, especially Stoicism”).

2. Vectorization and storage: Extracted facts and summaries are converted from textual form into numerical representations, so-called vector embeddings. Each embedding is a vector, that is, a series of numbers that represents the position of the given information in a multidimensional semantic space. This vector can be understood as a unique “semantic imprint” of the information. The data converted in this way is stored in the vector database, where each vector remains permanently recorded and linked to the user’s identity.

Vector embedding / embedding: Numerical representation of a text, word, sentence or document in the form of a sequence of numbers (vector) located in a multidimensional semantic space; semantically similar content has close vectors, allowing search by meaning instead of exact word match.

3. Context retrieval and enrichment: Before processing a new user query, the agent first searches the vector database. The search is not performed by keywords, but by semantic similarity. The agent converts the user’s current query into a vector and then searches the database for stored vectors (memories) that are closest to it in the semantic space. For example, if the user asks “Can you recommend me a new book following the ones we talked about earlier?”, the agent will recognize the semantic closeness of that query with the stored fact “The user is interested in ancient philosophy, especially Stoicism”. The most relevant records found are retrieved from the database and inserted into the context window along with the new query. In this way, the language model obtains key information from “long-term memory” that it needs to generate a relevant and personalized response (Xu et al., 2023).

This complex mechanism allows the agent to transcend its innate ahistorical nature. Having gone beyond the status of a linguistic automaton that reacts to the current stimulus, it becomes an interlocutor that “remembers” the shared history of interactions, respects the user’s specificities and thereby creates a basis for a continuous, consistent and ultimately more meaningful relationship.

6.3.3 Epistemic grounding: retrieval-enriched generation (RAG)

The Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) approach represents an important paradigm in the field of artificial intelligence, designed for the epistemic grounding of responses generated by large language models (LLM). It is a hybrid system that combines two basic components: a mechanism for retrieving data (retriever) and a generative language model (generator). The goal of such systems is to overcome the limitations of independent language models by combining their ability to shape language with the reliability and up-to-dateness of external knowledge bases.

RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation – a hybrid system that first retrieves relevant parts from an external knowledge base (retriever) to answer a user’s query, then passes that data and the query to a language model (generator) that synthesizes the final answer; this improves the timeliness and validity of the answers.

The need for this approach stems from two fundamental shortcomings of independent large language models. The first disadvantage is the tendency to “hallucinate”, that is, to generate factually incorrect or completely fabricated information, which happens when the model does not have the required information in its internal parameters. Another key disadvantage is the static nature of their knowledge base, which is limited to the data on which they have been trained and therefore does not include events or knowledge generated after their training is complete. The RAG system operation process itself can be broken down into several key steps. The cycle starts with a user query. This query is then forwarded to the retrieval component (retriever), whose task is to search the external knowledge base - for example, a collection of documents, a database or Internet sources - in order to find the most relevant parts of the text or data related to the set query. This found, relevant data together with the original user query forms an enriched context that is passed to the generative language model. In the final stage, the language model (generator) synthesizes the final answer, basing it on the obtained relevant data, and not exclusively on its internal, parametric knowledge.

Figure 6.5: Schematic representation of the operation of the RAG system.

The application of RAG architecture brings multiple advantages. The most important thing is the significant reduction in the occurrence of hallucinations, because the model directly relies on concrete, retrieved data when generating answers. Furthermore, RAG allows models to access updated or domain-specific, adapted information without the need for costly and time-consuming retraining of the entire model. This opens up the possibility of transparency and verifiability; along with the generated answer, the user can be offered the sources from which the information was taken, which allows him to check their accuracy himself. This approach is also more economical because updating the external knowledge base is much simpler and cheaper than retraining the entire language model (Lewis et al., 2020). In the context of more complex systems, such as autonomous agents, RAG assumes the role of a key tool for informed action. When an agent is faced with a task that requires reliable and up-to-date information, it does not act hastily, but relies on the RAG mechanism to gather relevant knowledge before making a decision or formulating a response. This ensures that the agent’s actions – whether it’s responding to a customer’s help desk inquiry or collecting data for more complex analysis – are not based on potentially outdated or inaccurate internal knowledge, but on verifiable external sources. It should be emphasized that although the core concept of the RAG architecture is extremely powerful, its naive or simplistic application often proves insufficient for more complex problems. Therefore, a whole spectrum of advanced techniques has been developed that optimize each stage of the described process. Today, this area represents one of the most dynamic fields of research in the development of artificial intelligence (Gao et al., 2024; Barnett et al., 2024). Advanced methods of indexing and searching, techniques of intelligent classification (reranking) of retrieved documents by importance, as well as strategies for summarizing and synthesizing information from several different sources are being researched.

6.3.4 Hands for action: using tools as a leap in power

Tool Use: The AI agent’s ability to call external tools (APIs, search engines, calculators, databases) during task execution; the model decides when and which tool to call, passes parameters, and uses the result to continue reasoning; a key component of agent architectures (e.g. ReAct).

The human hand, viewed in its anatomical and functional complexity, goes beyond the role of a grasping organ and asserts itself as primarily a tool of action. Her ability for fine motor adaptation, precise manipulation and firm grip is a fundamental prerequisite for one of the most important transitions in human development: the conscious use of tools. With this act, man becomes a being who actively shapes, adapts and transcends the world. Serving as a tool therefore represents a radical change in the relationship between man and the world, a true step forward in power that opens the way to the construction of culture and technology. This transformation deeply affects the very structure of human perception. Philosophical phenomenology has offered insightful insights into the nature of that process. Martin Heidegger introduces a distinction between tools as something ready-to-hand (German Zuhandenheit) and objects as something simply present (German Vorhandenheit). When we skillfully use a hammer, it does not exist for our consciousness as a separate object with certain properties, but recedes into the background and becomes an imperceptible extension of our hand focused on the act of driving a nail. The tool, fused with action, becomes transparent and opens the world to us not as a collection of objects to observe, but as a field of possibilities for action. On this track, Maurice Merleau-Ponty (1962) further develops the thought of the embodiment of the tool, arguing that the body includes it in its own body scheme. The classic example of the blind man’s cane clearly shows this phenomenon: for the blind man, the cane is an extension of his sensory apparatus with which he feels and explores the space in front of him. The tip of the stick becomes the new boundary of his body. In this way, the tool is transformed from an external object into an integral part of a person’s perceptive and active field.

Through this process of fusion of body and tool, man is transformed into a significantly more powerful agent. His relationship with the world is no longer determined solely by the biological limits of his body. The ax extends the strength and reach of the hand, the spear enables hunting at a distance, and the letter transcends the transience of speech and memory. Each new tool opens up new ways of being in the world and acting on it. This fundamental ability to use tools is therefore found at the very origin of human history as a history of creation, transformation and overcoming the given, confirming man as a being who is constantly rebuilding his world.

Figure 6.6: Expanding action by adopting tools: by integrating tools, the agent expands the action space and increases effectiveness.
